item.content:encoded:
Multiple skyscrapers and smaller structures have been constructed since the terrorist attacks on 11 September 2001 devastated Lower Manhattan. Here, we take a look at the site 25 years on.

In 1973, the World Trade Center complex comprised seven skyscrapers, including One and Two World Trade Center, the tallest buildings in the world at the time. All were destroyed in the terrorist attacks.

A quarter-century later, the site is now home to mostly glass-clad structures by some of the world's most famous architects.

Because of complicated jurisdiction, the rebuilding process took years, and the consortium of developers and governmental parties finally settled on a master plan by Studio Libeskind.

"I think that the impact [of 9/11] was on the whole world," Daniel Libeskind told Dezeen in 2021. "Everything changed in architecture after that. People were no longer willing to do it as before."

Beyond the infrastructural damage, the attacks reshaped the landscape of Lower Manhattan, including creating a toxic environment in the air in the surrounding parts of the city, the extent of which was recently released by the city government.

The rebuilding process began in earnest shortly after and continues today. Most of the planned buildings, except for the on-hold 5 WTC, have been completed.

In addition to the buildings listed below, other parks and city facilities were constructed.

Read on for the major buildings on the World Trade Center site. 

7 World Trade, SOM, 2006

Because it was technically outside of the Port Authority jurisdiction that the rest of the complex falls under, 7 World Trade was able to be rebuilt almost immediately after cleanup from the attacks had officially concluded, in 2002.

Designed by iconic skyscraper architect David Childs, it is a quiet and functional building and at 745 feet tall (227 metres), it is dwarfed by the other skyscrapers on the site. The original 7 WTC building interrupted the grid, but the grid around it was considered with the overall masterplan, and today Greenwich Street passes through the complex.

The National 9/11 Memorial, by Michael Arad/Handel Architects and Peter Walker, 2011

Ten years after the attacks, a memorial was completed on the site by a relatively unknown architect, Michael Arad, who embedded with Handel Architects to complete the structure despite disagreements between the stakeholders.

Today, the site has two granite-lined pits on the footprints of the Twin Towers and groves of trees in a park designed by Walker. The names of the victims were engraved into a parapet surrounding the site.

An underground museum designed by Davis Brody Bond with a panelled entry structure by Snøhetta also sits in the park and was completed in 2o14.

Find out more about the National 9/11 Memorial ›

Fiterman Hall, Pei Cobb Freed and Partners, 2012

An academic building, Fiterman Hall was first built in the late 1950s and was heavily damaged by debris during the attacks.

After it was demolished in 2009, Pei Cobb Freed and Partners built a brick-clad building with a recessed entry to serve the student population.

Four World Trade, by Fumihiko Maki, 2013

Designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, Four World Trade was the first of the skyscrapers under the Libeskind masterplan to be completed.

In line with 2010s skyscraper construction, it is covered in a glass curtain wall with an unusual single setback on one side where the upper portion slims and is trapezoidal. It rises 978 feet (298 metres).

One World Trade Center, by SOM, 2014

When it opened in 2014, One World Trade Center, once called Freedom Tower, was the tallest skyscraper in the Western Hemisphere and also the most expensive skyscraper ever built. Its height of 1776 feet (541 metres) was helped along by the massive antenna at its crown.

SOM's design replaced an initial design by Libeskind.

It has a faceted glass-covered facade and, because of security concerns, its base is clad in concrete and drapped in metal panels, which help integrate the base visually with the tower.

Find out more about One World Trade › 

World Trade Center Transportation Hub, by Santiago Calatrava, 2016

Serving as a connector for interstate transport, this transportation hub came to be called the Oculus and features massive steel ribs that cover the facade and extend outwards over the streets.

It features lofty internal spaces and skylights along the spine of the building that bring light into the spaces below, as most of the station is underground.

Find out more about The Oculus ›

Three World Trade, Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners, 2018

More than 15 years after the attacks, a 1,079-foot-tall (329 metres) skyscraper led by British architect Richard Rogers opened on the site.

Also mostly clad in glass, the building features steel bracing that run up the facade. The tower went up directly next to the Maki structure, making them appear as a pair, with similar dimensions on the glass window panelling.

Find out more about Three World Trade ›

St Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church, by Santiago Calatrava, 2022

Built to replace a church on the site this building is raised off the ground because of a security centre underneath.

It was informed by Byzantine architecture and features thin sheets of Pentelic marble that allow the structure to be illuminated from the inside at night.

Find out more about St Nicholas Greet Orthodox Church ›

Perelman Performing Arts Center, by Rex, 2023

Sited directly next to One World Trade, the Perelman Center sits on a plinth above the ground, in part because of the Port Authority infrastructure below. Architecture studio Rex had to deal with these constraints as well as the groundwork for a Frank Gehry building that was originally planned for the site.

Like St Nicholas,  the cubic structure is clad in thin marble that allows it to be illuminated. It has a series of modular theatre spaces inside.

Find out more about the Perelman Center ›

Two World Trade Center, by Foster + Partners, 2031 (planned)

Two World Trade Center could be the final piece in the decades-long development puzzle that is the World Trade Center site.

The glass-clad skyscraper will rise 1,226 feet (373 metres) and step up towards the crown. The design has been in contension with Foster + Parnters being replaced by BIG and then being reinstated. The studio released new renderings of the skyscraper before it broke ground in July 2026.

Find out more about Two World Trade Center ›

Dezeen Showroom: from pieces designed to blend into the background to others that make a visual statement, the following storage products conceal clutter within capacious forms.

These products come from the catalogues of global design brands, including those based in Denmark, Italy, the UK, Germany, South Korea and Poland.

The selection includes cabinets, cupboards, sideboards, and storage systems, both built-in and freestanding, available in neutral and pop colourways.

Dezeen Showroom publishes furnishings and products designed and manufactured by international design brands.

Wardrobes and storage by Reform

Danish brand Reform's wardrobes and storage have a slimline and fully customisable appearance, both inside and out.

Optional add-ons include accessories, drawers and organisers, with units varying in capacity, dimension and exterior colour, from natural neutrals to vivid block colours.

Find out more about Reform's wardrobes and storage ›

Container sideboard by E-ggs for Miniforms

Italian furniture brand Miniforms worked with design studio E-ggs on this sideboard, which has a rigid front and is raised on slim legs at each corner.

The exterior of the ContainerUP and ContainerMID sideboards comes in wooden or lacquered finishes, with users able to choose different colours for different elements to encourage personalisation.

Find out more about Container ›

MultiDrawer storage by Bisley

British workplace brand Bisley's MultiDrawer storage items are timeless thanks to their minimalist design and durability.

The filing cabinet-like pieces come in various colourways, heights and sizes, including limited edition ranges.

Find out more about MultiDrawer ›

Stripes storage system by Jehs + Laub for Schönbuch

New finishes and accent colours are available for German furniture brand Schönbuch and designers Jehs + Laub's Stripes storage system.

Named after the linear recesses in its fronts that act as handles, the system comprises freestanding and built-in modules that can be tailored to existing interiors.

Find out more about Stripes ›

DOB Modular System by Flat Point

South Korean brand Flat Point's DOB Modular System is made up of moveable elements ranging from side and console tables of various sizes and colours.

All pieces are made from aluminium and feature both open shelving alongside cupboards and drawers.

Find out more about DOB Modular System ›

Polish design brand Tylko invited users to utilise an online configurator to design their own storage systems made up of modules in the brand's Original Modern Shelving range.

From individual TV stands to full interior fit-outs, the system comes in a spectrum of colours and includes bookcases, sideboards, chests of drawers, vinyl storage and shoe racks.

item.content:encoded:
An "angled, folded form" clad in charred cedar defines this holiday home, designed by Japanese studio Keiji Ashizawa Design to embrace the surrounding landscape while maintaining its inhabitants' privacy.

The studio designed the 225-square-metre holiday home for a family to use either alone or with guests.

Located on the Yatsugatake mountain plateau in central Japan, the house has an unusual shape that was designed to suit its surroundings.

"Although surrounded by abundant nature, the site sits within a residential area of holiday homes," studio founder Keiji Ashizawa told Dezeen.

"The house was carefully positioned and shaped to remain open to the surrounding landscape while avoiding direct views toward neighbouring properties," Ashizawa continued.

"The placement of the windows follows the same approach, framing nature while maintaining a sense of privacy."

The one-storey building has a gentle bend that creates angles that enclose its garden.

"In response to the surrounding views, the movement of natural light, and the scale of the house in relation to the landscape, an angled, folded form was developed to sit naturally within the site," Ashizawa said.

House in Yatsugatake was clad in yakisugi, a traditional Japanese charred cedar. The material was allowed to be used because the home is not in a densely populated area, where Japan has strict fire regulations.

"Unlike in central Tokyo, timber cladding is permitted in this area, allowing yakisugi to form an integral part of the exterior expression," Ashizawa said.

Ashizawa's studio also took the climate of the region into consideration when designing the house, which is located close to the road and also contains a garage.

"The house rests on a concrete foundation that becomes more exposed as the ground falls away across the sloping site," Ashizawa said.

Read:

Keiji Ashizawa creates holiday home within historic machiya

"Its relatively high profile also responds to the winter snowfall of Yatsugatake, following a construction approach commonly found in timber houses in colder regions," Ashizawa continued.

The holiday home has a central entrance, with a living, dining and kitchen area, loft and guest room in the western wing and private rooms and bathrooms to the east.

Keiji Ashizawa Design used oak wood for the interior, which features exposed sloping beams and windows close to the roof that frame the garden.

A skylight above the mezzanine loft lets light into the living room area.

To create a connection with the garden, the studio added full-width timber-framed windows in the bathroom that give panoramic views of the surrounding forest.

"By carefully reading the existing topography, trees, light, and wind, and allowing the architecture to respond quietly to them, we sought to create a home in which the surrounding landscape gradually reveals itself over time," the studio said.

Keiji Ashizawa Design has previously created an eight-room Tokyo hotel and a holiday home in a historic machiya.

The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku.

Project architect: Keiji Ashizawa, Kenji Kawami
Structural engineer: AS Associates, Akira Suzuki
Construction: Tanaka Jyuuken Co Ltd

item.content:encoded:
London may have a lot to shout about design-wise, but is it actually possible to survive as a creative in one of the world's most expensive cities? Ahead of London Design Festival, we spoke to five local designers about the challenges they face.

"I'm willing to live very modestly" said Tessa Silva

"Financially, I've had the toughest start to the year that I've had in the 10 years since graduating. I was teaching and assisting another artist before, I had my finger in a couple of other pies, but I let it all fall by the wayside. I suddenly found myself in a position where I didn't have anything to fall back on. It's taught me I have to keep connections with people and let them know I can still work for them, even if it seems like I have a big commission.

"Any time I do make money, I put it back into making new things in my studio. I'm willing to live very modestly, and hopefully that pays off one day. I don't buy new clothes or go out for dinner a lot; I make my own packed lunches. I live in a small flat that I've made beautiful – that's just part of choosing to live in London.

"A good currency for designers is doing swaps with people. I've gotten a photographer to photograph my work because I've given them a piece of my furniture, or I've got some nice jewellery because I've swapped it for work. It's a way of owning a few precious things when you can't afford to pay upfront for them.

"Even though this year has been really hard, I've been getting a few bites this summer that are making me excited and make me think this could be something long term and sustainable for the future, which is a really nice feeling."

Tessa Silva is exhibiting at Max Radford Gallery's Progressive Permanence

"You find nifty ways of transporting wood when you're going on a bike everywhere" said Jake Robertson

"Work for a designer who's got plenty of work for you to do, and they might be keen for you to use their workshop in your spare time – that's what James Shaw has done for me. I had to get inventive and learn how to make stuff that can fold up, disappear, and slip into the cracks of the workshop so I'm not taking up someone's space. It does mean you've got to graft outside of work and on the weekend, but it gave me access to great machinery.

"A great place to go for cheap offcut materials is Renée Materials. You'll find stuff there that you would never think could make furniture. I cycle – I'm not paying for transport, I can't do it – but you find nifty ways of transporting wood when you're going on a bike everywhere.

"I don't really make money from my practice. I've sold a couple of things, but it's not a money-making business. Hopefully one day I can get there, but that's a reason I would suggest people work part-time or full-time for a designer. I don't have to keep pumping my own work out. I also need a job that pays the rent. I can make good work and keep putting those things out – I don't need to dilute my Instagram by constantly putting stuff out for likes when that doesn't equal more sales."

Jake Robertson is exhibiting at Out of Worky and Design Everything's With Limitations

"My hack is trying to overcome my feeling of cringe" said Hanna Fastrich

"There are a lot of challenges in London, but it's a super-rich environment, and what's most important to me is my community. I have friends from uni or group exhibitions that are also designers, and we support each other. I work on ceramics and metal in my workshop, and sometimes I want to do some wood or something else, which a friend can give me access to. There's a beautiful sharing economy in my community – there's no gatekeeping.

"I always intensely apply to open calls, prizes and grants. I get loads of rejections, but every once in a while you get a yes. In the beginning, it felt cringe to reach out to people or send an email with my portfolio to a gallery, so my hack is trying to overcome my feeling of cringe and not to think about the worst possible outcome. Someone could say no and reject you, but that's not a horrible outcome, it's just a numbers game in the end."

Hanna Fastrich is exhibiting at Slancha's Hanging Baskets

"I turned to using waste materials as a necessity" said ThisIsByron

"My biggest overhead is material costs. That's how I turned to using waste materials – as a necessity. I then looked at what I could find within London and made a patchwork series with hardwood offcuts I found from various studios.

"I currently have a part-time job at the Royal Academy Schools as a workshop tutor. It's important I earn a wage that supports London living but also pays back into my studio.

"London is tricky, but it's also a bit of magic. Unit.d in Haggerston is like a church service affair where designers descend each month to hang out and share ideas – this only exists because of living in the city."

ThisIsByron is curating We Lift Each Other

"It's more valuable to have relationships with expert makers" said Marc Sweeney

"After I graduated in London, I moved back to Scotland and quickly discovered that I wasn't part of any design community. I may as well have been making work on the moon – there's just no point doing it if nobody's engaging with you.

"I am wrestling with the balance of being in London to network and work freelance, and I'm going to be teaching at Instituto Marangoni, then coming up to Scotland to make things. My family runs a passenger boat business on Loch Lomond, so we've got unbelievable workshop facilities. The long-term plan is to have a space in London, but it is eye-wateringly expensive – almost pretty much unaffordable for a single emerging designer.

"I'm a hands-on maker, but my work's got to a point where I need the help of experts. I'm outsourcing some work, or certain stages of my work. It's more valuable to have relationships with expert makers, which there are loads of in London, than it is to have your own space with machinery and you're trying to do absolutely everything yourself."

Marc Sweeney is exhibiting at Slancha's Hanging Baskets

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: the rugged aesthetic of the Australian outback meets the sophistication of contemporary design in the Cattle armchair, created by Gibson Karlo for the brand Design By Them.

Karlo took inspiration from the industrial metalwork seen on structures such as silos in the Australian rural landscape for the Cattle chair, adapting a style of joint where tubular metal is flattened and screwed together at points of intersection.

The usually rugged joint is given a refined and softened interpretation in the chair, combined with invisible connections and high-gloss finish in two refined shades: Merlot and Camel.

"The compressed tubular connection is a process rooted in agricultural metalwork," said Karlo. "We refined the typically harsh transition between round tube and flat surface, allowing the two forms to flow together and making the join a defining feature of the piece."

The Cattle chair's steel frame is paired with plush upholstered cushioning that drapes over the armrests and backrests.

The upholstery is available in a curated selection of fabrics from leading textile brands Kvadrat and Maharam.

item.content:encoded:
The Craft x Tech exhibition at the V&A will see artisans from Japan's Tokai region collaborate with international designers, including Philippe Malouin and Bethan Laura Wood, for London Design Festival.

The project aims to explore how traditional craft techniques can be used in new ways to create contemporary designs.

"We are not necessarily looking for the most famous crafts, but for techniques that seem to contain possibilities that have not yet been fully explored," Craft x Tech founder Hideki Yoshimoto, who worked on the project with curatorial director Maria Cristina Didero, told Dezeen.

"A craft may have developed over hundreds of years for a very particular purpose, but the knowledge accumulated within it can often have a much wider relevance than the objects it traditionally produces."

This year's edition of Craft x Tech, which first launched in 2024, focuses on craftsmanship from Japan's Tokai region.

It sees David Caon work with Yohei Ito, Lanzavecchia + Wai with Takanori Senda, Wood with Hiroyuki Murase, Malouin with Shigeyuki Ando, Eugene Kangawa with Mayuki Kato and Atang Tshikare with Tomoyuki Matsuda.

The aim was to not make the pairing of the designers and craftspeople "too obvious," Yoshimoto said.

"A certain distance between the designer and the craftsperson is useful: rather than simply applying a new design to an existing technique, they have to find their own point of connection, and that is often where something genuinely new begins," he explained.

For the designers, the collaboration provided an opportunity to work in new ways.

Industrial designer Caon, who created the Fushi modular ceramic console and lighting piece together with Ito of ceramic brand Fudogama, said he designed the original concept and this was then adapted by Ito.

"The original vision and the resulting piece are very different, but the spirit has been preserved by the understanding we both developed through our collaboration," Caon told Dezeen.

"Fushi is a piece created very much in my own language, but the distinct and beautiful green glaze and, indeed, the precision of the pieces is representative of Fudogama craftsmanship."

The resulting piece uses traditional oribe glaze to dramatic effect.

"The individual modules that make up the final assemblages are made to be identical," Caon said. "The oribe glaze, however, reacts completely unpredictably, removing any sense of uniformity across the surface of the piece."

Read:

Fourteen must-see exhibitions and installations at London Design Festival 2026

Also taking part in the exhibition is UK designer Wood, whose Kataginu light collection with artisan Murase of textile company Suzusan "celebrates the 'magic' of tying, binding and folding at the heart of the shibori dyeing technique," Wood told Dezeen.

Named for kataginu, a traditional Japanese sleeveless vest, the colourful lampshades have sculptural forms that also draw on rain chains, temple roofs and folded paper masks.

They were made using a dying technique called arimatsu narumi shibori, which also influenced the final design.

"The design process establishes a direct connection between three-dimensional folded construction, the resulting dyed pattern, and the final form of each light," Wood said.

"Central to the collection is an exploration of the unpredictable colour transitions that occur when two dyes interact, capturing the 'living' quality of the dye as it responds to folding, binding and manipulation."

Her work was partly informed by previous designs by Suzusan that had also used textiles.

"I wanted to expand on this and develop the textile and bespoke lighting component together to make a family of lighting that combined the final results of shibori alongside keeping elements of the folding, stitching and binding that are normally removed during the process," Wood said.

"I worked with Suzusan to choose colours that also reacted well when illuminated – I love that the soft gentle pastel pink transforms into an almost neon colour when lit."

French designer Malouin wanted his Kasane design, made with Ando of the Aichi Prefecture brand Ando Cloisonne, to be closely connected to the brand's language but reinterpreted through his own approach.

"I wanted the result to feel contemporary without being disconnected from what they traditionally produce," Malouin told Dezeen. "The final design is a series of functional boxes which, when stacked together, form a sculptural totem."

The restraints of the process also had an effect on the design process, with Malouin deciding to make smaller items than he had first wanted due to the size of the kiln.

The designer, who says his work is "rarely decorative" worked with Ando to find the right approach to the surface decoration of the vessels.

"I wrapped sheets of paper around full-scale models of the boxes and marked them freely and almost randomly with a large felt-tip pen," Malouin said.

This led to an unusual design with an "intuitive" feel that represented both Malouin's designs and Ando Cloisonne's craftsmanship.

"The final objects bring together the simplicity of my forms and mark-making with the extraordinary precision and care of Shigeyuki Ando’s cloisonné technique," Malouin said.

"There is something surprising about seeing such a spontaneous, handmade pattern translated through such a meticulous and highly skilled process. That contrast is where the design represents us both."

Also on show at LDF is a collection of reinterpreted Marcel Breuer furniture and many, many more must-see installations, as chosen by the Dezeen team.

The photography is by Masayuki Hayashi.

item.content:encoded:
French design studio Uchronia drew inspiration from the historic architecture of the Grand Palais museum when creating this monumental floral installation that will be on display throughout Paris Design Week.

Le Grand Bouquet is located at the heart of the Antin Rotunda and was designed by Uchronia to reference the space's mosaic floor, as well as the decorative mouldings that adorn the arcades.

Uchronia founder Julien Sebban was asked by the Grand Palais and Paris Design Week to create a sculptural intervention that would complement the architecture of the recently restored building, rather than simply occupying it.

"We wanted the installation to feel as though it had grown from the Grand Palais itself, while bringing the joyful, colourful and slightly surreal language of Uchronia into this very historic setting," Sebban told Dezeen.

The large-scale metal sculpture draws inspiration from the rotunda's floral decorations and exaggerates them to create a new architectural expression that is in dialogue with its surroundings.

The stylised petals seem to emerge from the floor, while the circular composition echoes the geometry of the rotunda, guiding the eye upwards to the ornate ceiling.

"We imagined it almost as an extension of the building, as though the ornamentation had suddenly started growing and taken over the room," Sebban said.

The designer claimed that, despite its monumental scale, the piece was designed to feel "generous, playful and accessible", which is achieved in part by the visual lightness and fragility of the flowers.

Uchronia collaborated closely with a range of French artisans to create the installation, including metalworkers at metal workshop Atelier François Pouenat, who developed the internal metal structure.

Paint and coatings specialists Seigneurie helped bring colour to the sculpture, using the PPG Group's Chromatic paint to achieve a luminous glossy finish.

The base of the sculpture is surrounded by circular beds, made by bed brand Tréca Paris and upholstered by silk weaver Manufacture Prelle, which encourage visitors to pause and contemplate the rotunda's architecture.

Read:

Uchronia creates giant four-poster bed for Paris Design Week

"We didn't want Le Grand Bouquet to be something that visitors only looked at from a distance – we wanted people to inhabit it," said Sebban.

"The beds introduce an unexpected domestic gesture into the monumental scale of the Grand Palais, while the silk upholstery brings another layer of softness, tactility and French craftsmanship to the experience."

Dotted around the space is furniture created by Uchronia for French design brand Tiptoe, including tables featuring FENIX surfaces produced by materials brand Arpa Industriale.

The installation is accompanied by a colourful inflatable structure outside the building, which welcomes visitors and creates a threshold between the city and the playful interior space.

Le Grand Bouquet is free to visit throughout Paris Design Week, and Sebban said he hopes visitors will leave "feeling a bit lighter than when they arrived."

"The project is about joy as a form of resistance and as something capable of bringing people together," he added.

"In a period often defined by uncertainty, we wanted to make something unapologetically optimistic – an installation that celebrates beauty, imagination and the pleasure of sharing an experience with other people."

Le Grand Bouquet is on show as part of the Grand Palais Design and Arts and Crafts Boutique, which offers a curated selection of exclusive design objects celebrating craftsmanship and innovation.

The Grand Palais underwent a comprehensive renovation led by French studio Chatillon Architectes that modernised its galleries, some of which are being temporarily occupied by the Centre Pompidou as it undergoes its own restoration.

Le Grand Bouquet is typical of Uchronia's playful signature style, which combines colour, vegetal forms, craftsmanship and storytelling to create designs for objects and spaces that incite emotion in their users.

The studio, which Sebban founded in 2019, previously created another Paris Design Week installation comprising a monumental bed informed by the interiors of the 18th-century Hôtel de la Marine.

Other projects include a cafe interior in Paris designed to evoke a traditional Korean house and a psychedelic boutique in London featuring a floor made from painted lava stone.

The photography is by Romain Moriceau.

Le Grand Bouquet is on show from 11 to 20 September at Grand Palais, Paris. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.

item.content:encoded:
Two accessory dwelling units are contained within a double-level, arched metal building, which was created by design-build studo Qastic.

The project is located in a residential neighbourhood dominated by low-rise homes with pitched roofs.

For a rectangular site with a main house, local studio Qastic set out to create two ADUs within a compact footprint of 1,500 square feet (140 square metres).

The team conceived a pair of arched metal volumes that resemble Quonset huts, with one stacked atop the other at a perpendicular angle.

Drawing upon the local context, the design rethinks the traditional pitched-roof structure.

"Rather than rejecting this familiar typology, the design transforms it into a continuous vaulted form, maintaining the functional logic of water drainage while introducing a more efficient and spatially generous geometry," the team said.

"Designed to accommodate two independent households within a limited footprint, the project proposes a flexible model for increasing density in low-rise residential neighbourhoods."

The building has a steel frame and is wrapped in white-painted, galvanised Purlin Bearing Rib (PBR) panels. The cladding forms a reflective "cool" roof system that is well suited to the warm climate of Southern California.

Each level of the building contains an ADU with its own entry, according to Qastic. A central enclosed stair provides access to the upper level.

Units contain an open room for cooking, dining and lounging, along with a bedroom and bathroom. Standard finishes include timber flooring and drywall.

Read:

Ten American ADUs that showcase their urban versatility

Balconies in the upper unit offer views of the distant city skyline, while patios in the lower unit connect to the site's landscaping.

The building's vaulted form reduces material usage while also improving building performance, according to the team.

"At the same time, the curved ceilings generate more expansive interior volumes, increasing daylight penetration and spatial continuity within a compact plan," the team said.

While designed for two distinct households, the building could become a single-family home.

"Each unit operates independently, with separate access and outdoor space, but can also function as a single dwelling if required," the team said.

"This dual condition allows the building to adapt to changing household structures over time."

Qastic said its goal was to explore how "geometry, economy and social flexibility" could come together in one urban building.

"Casa Plus presents an alternative approach to small-scale housing in Los Angeles, combining compact planning with spatial adaptability in response to increasing urban density," the studio said.

Other ADUs in Los Angeles include a sculptural building by Byben with ipe wood cladding and curved elements, and a blue building by Assembledge+ that features an asymmetrical gabled roof.

The photography is by Mohamad Momenabadi, Sayeh Moomsaz and Mahdi A Bakhshian.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a "cohesive yet layered industrial cluster" of boatyard buildings on Bristol's harbourside is among the architecture projects from Cardiff University.

Also featured is the concept of a neurodivergent-informed kitchen-garden school and a proposal for a women's housing scheme geared towards single mothers and older women.

Cardiff University

Institution: Cardiff University
School: Welsh School of Architecture
Course: BSc Architecture

School statement:

"The Welsh School of Architecture (WSA), based in Cardiff, is a world-renowned institution for design and built environment studies.

"Originally founded over a century ago, the WSA has a strong tradition of excellence in architectural education.

"Our teaching and research embrace the diversity and transdisciplinary nature of architecture – we foster curious, creative, critical, ethical learners who can approach challenges with wide-ranging, flexible skills and knowledge.

"Our vision is to contribute to the making of built environments that enhance the wellbeing of current and future generations while caring for the planet.

"The BSc in Architecture is a three-year undergraduate degree course accredited by RIBA, ARB and LAM (Malaysia). The programme covers design, technology, history, theory, representation and professional practice dimensions of the architectural discipline.

"Through studio projects, we encourage our students to take a holistic view of how buildings are designed, used, made and what their broader impacts are, whilst fostering an ethos of 'grounded creativity', exposing students to real world sites and live challenges as the basis for design projects.

"These approaches are reflected in the range of our year three design units, each of which empowers students to explore and tackle pressing issues for architecture, cities and society."

A Common Ground – The Talgarth School of Cooking by Olivia Liggins

"A Common Ground is a proposal for a kitchen-garden school that places the neurodivergent user at the centre of the design process.

"Rather than treating neurodiversity as a constraint, the project embraces it as a driver for architectural decision-making, creating environments that prioritise autonomy and wellbeing.

"Through a series of interconnected spaces, the building supports varying levels of sensory engagement, allowing users to navigate between moments of activity and retreat without compromising their sense of belonging.

"The project demonstrates how architecture can foster confidence, independence and meaningful social connection through an inclusive and human-centred approach to design."

Student: Olivia Liggins
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutor: Michael Corr
Email: oliviasianliggins[at]gmail.com

The Domestic Collective: A Feminist Co-Housing Model by Lucy Hilton

"The Domestic Collective proposes a women's housing scheme in Ross-on-Wye for single mothers and older women, informed by research into perceived safety and feminist spatial theory.

"It explores how architecture can prioritise visibility, community and collectivisation of domesticity.

"Organised around a sequence of courtyards and communal facilities including a laundrette, kitchen and nursery, the design promotes interaction, mutual support and natural surveillance.

"Strategies including long sightlines, active thresholds, and integrated lighting enhance safety, while shared resources reduce isolation and labour duplication.

"The project reinterprets the site's history as a former gasworks into a centre of light, exchange and empowerment."

Student: Lucy Hilton
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Elliott Wang and Matthew Whittaker
Email: lucyhitlon1[at]icloud.com

The Living Archives by Sam Stevens

"Challenging rigid housing models in Ross-on-Wye, this proposal embraces the chaotic reality of domesticity.

"Through the adaptive reuse of an existing garage, the project anchors a localised circular economy via the 'collective exchange' – a public library for renting and repairing household items.

"The scheme bridges young families and professionals through an incentivised co-living framework, exchanging domestic support for reduced rent.

"Spatially, the architecture invites functional 'misuse'.

"Negotiable 'buffer zones' and unprogrammed Glulam 'intervention walls' replace static boundaries, empowering residents to actively adapt their spaces and leave an evolving, unpredictable mark on the building."

Student: Sam Stevens
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Elliott Wang and Matt Whittaker
Email: sam5t3v3n5[at]gmail.com

A Circular Assemblage by Jack Youell

"Located in Bristol's dockyard, the craft hub implements a strict 'waste-to-resource' logic to align with net-zero industry pressures. The scheme houses carpentry, glass and pottery workshops within a demountable brick-slip facade and modular timber frame.

"Spatially, inward-pitching roofs compress around a central working courtyard, guiding visitors through a narrative-driven material journey.

"This sequence transitions heavy industrial workflows into community infrastructure, utilising site-manufactured materials and products such as flitch beams to showcase the craft and reanimate its previous maritime presence.

"To reduce energy demands, a localised firing tower reclaims craft process heat to completely eliminate secondary, carbon-intensive heating, fusing sustainable production with public life."

Student: Jack Youell
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Jared Baron and Brendan Higgins
Email: jackyouell.design[at]gmail.com

Reinterpreting Obsolescence by Alfie Elliott

"Following the closure of traditional steelmaking at Port Talbot and the growing redundancy of city-centre parking, the project transforms Newport's Clarence Car Park into a public-facing centre for steel reuse.

"Retaining the existing concrete structure, it introduces low-carbon additions, including reclaimed steel from a nearby former steelworks and strawbale insulation.

"The proposal provides areas for industrial production, education and civic space, addressing a weak, existing steel reuse network in the UK and consequential public under-engagement.

"Through phased repair, reuse and retrofit, the building supports former steelworkers, encourages circular construction and offers a scalable model for reinterpreting obsolete structures and industries."

Student: Alfie Elliott
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Benjamin Wells and Hannah Summers
Email: alfieelliott21[at]icloud.com

Decay and Renewal: Layers of Repair by Laura Nolan

"This project acts as a direct intervention response to the decay of Clarence Place Car Park, with its preservation at the heart of the design.

"The low-value structure is reimagined as a civic hub through adaptive reuse.

"A permanent scaffold frame enables incremental repair before becoming part of the architecture through an additional metal skin.

"Workshop, education, and community spaces are introduced through phased occupation, inviting public participation in the building's transformation.

"Each layer of intervention remains legible, preserving traces of the past while allowing future adaptation, so the building continues to evolve as a lasting symbol of Newport's regeneration."

Student: Laura Nolan
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Hannah Summers and Benjamin Wells
Email: lauranolan500[at]gmail.com

Sanyukt Seva Kendra by Jaskaran Singh

"Sanyukt Seva Kendra (Shared Service Centre) explores how architecture can improve equitable access to essential services within rapidly urbanising cities.

"Located between Veraval and Somnath in Gujarat, India, the project responds to fragmented urban growth and uneven investment by proposing a dense civic hub where transport infrastructure becomes civic infrastructure.

"Combining healthcare, markets, offices and waste processing within a new transport interchange, it transforms everyday movement into opportunities for social and economic exchange.

"Climate-responsive design, permeable public spaces, and locally informed materials create an adaptable civic architecture that reconnects communities and demonstrates how infrastructure can support a more equitable city."

Student: Jaskaran Singh
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutor: Shibu Raman
Email: s.jaskaran20000[at]gmail.com

Anti-Oculus: The Centre of Injustice and Activism by Amos Shammai

"Cardiff's Temple of Peace and Health was built in 1938, permanently casting its self-proclaimed symbolism in concrete, right before the outbreak of world war two.

"This project contends that without justice, peace becomes mere ornament, especially as global instability renders such ideals increasingly abstract.

"The Anti-Oculus, a centre of injustice, receives its first case file, investigating spatial power and control through design, producing findings that dismantle and re-configure the fabric from which its inquiry emanates.

"The project rejects finality, identifying as an extra point in an expanding map charting the philosophy of escape and liberation."

Student: Amos Shammai
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Dimitra Ntzani and Caitlin Mullard
Email: amosshammai[at]gmail.com

River souvenirs by Toby Hope

"This year three architecture project proposes a material archive along the River Taff, positioned beside the Taff Trail in Cardiff.

"The archive collects and displays litter and industrial remnants recovered from the river, reflecting the environmental conditions and industrial history of the site.

"Acting as both exhibition and intervention, the project encourages local communities and passersby to engage with the materials, reconsider their relationship with the river, and inspire collective responsibility for maintaining and reconnecting Cardiff's vital access to the city's waterways."

Student: Toby Hope
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Hugo Keene and Aled Davies
Email: tobyhope128[at]gmail.com

The Underfall Collective by Scarlett Cowley

"My proposal, The Underfall Collective, reimagines this historic Bristol boatyard as a cohesive yet layered industrial cluster, using a distinctive red tiled facade to define key landmarks and entrances, balancing public and private access points, allowing different user groups to coexist and maintaining clear spatial boundaries.

"The scheme connects the public life of the boatyard with private workshop spaces, while supporting the preservation of endangered traditional crafts like wooden boat building via learning and apprenticeship environments.

"The site's relationship with the wider Bristol Western Harbour area is strengthened by a design that responds to both existing conditions and future development."

Student: Scarlett Cowley
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutors: Brendan Higgins, Akshara Pulpa, Richard O'Hanlon and Jed Baron
Email: scowleyhk[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
New York's Twin Towers were recreated with lighted drones to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, with each light representing a life lost.

Named 2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor, the installation on 9 September consisted of drones outlining the Twin Towers at full architectural scale. It was designed in collaboration with the 9/11 family, survivor, responder community with creative director Addison Mehr.

Drift (formerly Studio Drift) acted as advisors along with architects Shigeru Ban and Dean Maltz. Studio Drift said it represented "one of the most important remembrances of our lifetime" and noted the use of technology as a futuristic remembrance tool.

"We could not think of a more impactful use of technology as it is now more important than ever to create the best possible future by using the new tools of our time to never forget the past," said Studio Drift.

The light installation was illuminated twice, for fifteen minutes each time. Once the drones assembled, they hovered in the air over the New York Harbor for several minutes before the lights turned off and the drones returned to their landing spots.

Each of the 2,977 drones represented a life lost during the 9/11 terrorist attack on 11 September 2001. It was designed to be in dialogue with the Tribute in Light skylights that are projected from the Twin Towers site every year.

Read:

The National 9/11 Memorial was the most significant building of 2011

The team consulted with representatives of the family, survivors and emergency responders for the design.

"Like the landscape of New York City, memory and understanding of history are also shaped by and reflect constant change," said New York City Fire Department responder and artist Brenda Berkman.

"But art can help convey information, feelings and understanding of past events from one generation to the next."

The installation also included references to some of the alternative building proposals that arose in the wake of the incident.

According to the team, the "helix" of drones formed as the installation came together represented Think's unbuilt World Cultural Centre master plan proposal.

Ban worked on this proposal as a collaborator on a team called Think, which also included architects Rafael Viñoly and David Rockwell.

Studio Libeskind ultimately designed the master plan.

Read:

9/11 anniversary: how the World Trade Center site was rebuilt

Drift has created several drone installations, including a wavy shape above the Elbphilharmonie concert hall in Hamburg and shows for a version of the Burning Man festival after it was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021.

Dezeen previously examined the impact of 9/11 in a series dedicated to the event's 20th anniversary, while Foster + Partners released updated images of the final tower being built on the site, which is now under construction.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture studio Oatelier has completed Husárik Hut, a barn-like timber home in Slovakia that was designed as a contemporary take on the area's traditional shepherd's huts.

Perched on a sloping site overlooking the Javorníky mountain range, the home draws on the typical rural architecture of Slovakia's north-western Kysuce region, including shepherd's huts built from local materials.

"The starting point was not a nostalgic image of vernacular architecture, but the principles embedded within it – natural materials, familiar proportions, a simple gabled form and a close relationship with the landscape," Oatelier co-founder Martin Kvitkovský told Dezeen.

"It is intended to feel less like an object placed in the landscape and more like a continuation of it, a contemporary layer within a region that is changing, while retaining a strong sense of identity and continuity," he added.

Beyond mimicking the gabled timber form of these huts, Oatelier was interested in their historic internal layouts, in which several generations would typically occupy one large room.

This informed a desire to keep the home as open and connected as possible, with the living, dining and kitchen areas occupying a single room on the ground floor, centred around a fireplace.

This room expands into a double-height space to the east, which opens onto a large terrace perched above the sloping site. This terrace wraps around the home in a walkway sheltered by the projecting gable ends above.

On the first floor of Husárik Hut, the feeling of openness continues with a wide corridor positioned beneath the apex of a skylit gable ceiling and illuminated by square and circular windows at either end.

Rather than linking enclosed rooms, this corridor connects a series of what Kvitkovský calls "niches", containing a skylit study and bedrooms that can be closed off with curtains.

Read:

Slanted facade encloses modular Czech home by Papundekl Architects

"Instead of dividing the plan into conventional rooms, we created a continuous sequence of spaces that gradually change in scale, ceiling height and natural light," Kvitkovský explained.

"Niches, alcoves and smaller corners allow for moments of retreat without cutting inhabitants off from one another," he added. "The openness makes it possible to sense what is happening elsewhere in the house, maintaining a subtle awareness of the presence of others throughout the day."

An exposed timber structure frames the interiors, strengthened by thin beams and bracing in cream-painted steelwork.

Matching timber has been used for large sections of built-in storage, including double-height shelving in the living room that extends into a small nook with a daybed, and bedroom storage tucked beneath the sloping ceilings.

Externally, the base of the home is finished with horizontal timber battens while the gable ends above feature exposed framework, which is crowned by a large metal roof.

"The material palette grows directly from the local building culture. Timber and other natural materials establish a physical and visual connection with the Kysuce landscape and its traditional rural architecture," said Kvitkovský.

"At the same time, the construction is deliberately contemporary. The result is a timber structure that feels familiar in its setting while belonging clearly to the present," he added.

Other projects in Slovakia recently featured on Dezeen include a home in Bratislava by Čechvala Architects, which is comprised of a stack of three rectilinear volumes clad in corrugated aluminium, and a residence by Paulíny Hovorka Architects, which is hugged by a rocky garden.

The photography is by Peter Čintalan, courtesy of Dynameet Studio.

item.content:encoded:
Superflux co-founder Anab Jain has been awarded this year's LDF Design Innovation Medal. In this interview, she argues speculative design can still be a source of hope even in dark times.

It's yet another 32-degree day in London's alarming summer of 32-degree days, and Jain has been telling her colleagues about her childhood in India.

It was a time of national emergency, with food rationing due to drought and crop failures, water for only one hour a day, stifling heat – and yet, young Jain was happy.

"I still had the best childhood, in a way," she said.

"It makes me think a lot about how what we have assumed are the perfect conditions for us to live happily might not necessarily be so, and how that sort of living – growing up fairly frugally but very happily, with no television, no telephone, being bored out of our minds, cooking up stories, and reading a lot about Indian mythology because that's all that was around – really shaped my worldview."

That worldview, with hope and resilience peeking out from behind a profound understanding of crisis and scarcity, has subtly infused Jain's 17-year body of work, which has won her the London Design Festival's (LDF) Design Innovation Medal for 2026.

"What if AI was used in the service of our rivers?"

As part of Superflux, the design studio she started in 2009 with her life and creative partner Jon Ardern, Jain has repeatedly cast herself into the future, addressing the challenges of climate change and social upheaval through speculative propositions and ecological thinking.

In 2018, she gave a talk at the Interaction Design Association (IxDA) conference in Lyon, turning the field's guiding concept of human-centred design on its head by proposing a "more-than-human-centred design".

Drawing on the work of academic Anne Galloway and her More-Than-Human lab in New Zealand, Jain argued for a practice of listening to, working with and creating for the planet's interconnected species and natural entities. At that time, no one knew what she was talking about, she recalls.

But the next year, she gave a similar presentation at Madrid festival Tentacular to a crowd that included John Bridle, who was in the middle of writing what would become the influential book Ways of Being, exploring the intelligence of animals, plants and natural systems.

Shoots of like-minded thought, inspired by indigenous knowledge and rights of nature theory, were starting to look like a movement.

Seven years later, it is difficult to find a critical design thesis that does not at least touch on the notion of the more-than-human world.

The roots for all of this are embedded in Jain's formative years. After her summers of paucity, she went on to study film – an unusual speciality for the design field that was offered at Ahmedabad's National Institute of Design, the school set up on the advice of Charles and Ray Eames to combine modernist approaches with a focus on the needs and traditions of India.

Read:

Animal-centric interspecies design goes "beyond sustainability"

There, she was exposed to a great breadth of cinema, while also developing the skills that would inform the film, storytelling and experiential sides of Superflux's practice.

"We used to look at a lot of French cinema, a lot of Iranian cinema, a lot of Italian, Korean cinema," said Jain. "We didn't watch that much Hollywood."

"So in a way, I was aware of the fact that there are plural perspectives that exist in the world, that there are different stories that need to be heard and need to be told, and there is not just one way to be."

In 2008, after gaining her masters at the Royal College of Art in London, Jain went to work on machine intelligence at the Microsoft Research lab in Cambridge – the first place where she was prompted to think about intelligence in a non-human dimension.

Her experiences converge in Superflux projects such as the Ecological Intelligence Agency, which was included in last year's More Than Human exhibition at the Design Museum.

It started with a simple idea: "Instead of powering AI with natural resources, let's flip it, and ask what if AI was used in the service of our rivers and water systems instead," said Jain.

In the work, a large language model is fed multiple sources of data about Essex's River Roding, from ecological reports to community social media posts, and told to draw on English Romantic ballads, free verse poetry and the tongue of London spoken-word artists for style.

Then it is asked to speak for the river itself. Hearing this voice can be, for the listener, deeply moving, as well as a chance to envisage a radically different future for AI.

"In the short term, I think there's not much to be optimistic about"

Then there are the Mitigation of Shock installations – pragmatic imaginings of future apartments adapted for living with climate change.

In one version, heavy aluminium shutters provide protection from intense storms, while a kayak propped against a wall suggests how the residents travel through regular flooding.

At the same time, there are elements of what is sometimes termed 'hope-punk', such as bountiful indoor gardens that double as a reliable food supply.

The installation is emblematic of Superflux's version of optimism, based not on denial that climate chaos is coming, but on belief that human resilience, ingenuity and practices of care will shine through regardless.

Asked whether she stands by the defiant optimism she expressed then, Jain said: "In the short term, I think there's not much to be optimistic about, in all honesty."

She cites the widespread wildfires in Europe, energy challenges, proliferating wars, social disruption from AI and likely changes to the Atlantic current as reasons to be dour.

"These conditions point towards what you can call a closing down – more boundaries, people wanting to hold on to what they think is the right thing, the narrowing of possibilities, rather than an opening up of," she continued. "So, in these conditions, how can we be optimistic?"

This is where speculative design comes into its own. Previously at the margins of the design profession, the practice has recently become a part of its commercial sphere and looks increasingly like the approach best matched to the challenges of the present moment.

Here again, Jain has been an influential thinker, leading the Design Investigations course as a professor at the University of Applied Arts Vienna and this year, publishing the book Designing Questions with her colleagues to outline a pedagogic pathway for the field.

"The work we do as Superflux in terms of making sure the future remains a possibility space, and that there are many possible futures within this possibility space, gives me hope and optimism," said Jain.

"There is still a chance to imagine, will, prototype, create, test all these other possible futures."

One beautiful possibility? "We may not get 24/7 water, but we may live a more cohesive, collectively happier life."

item.content:encoded:
JW Anderson founder Jonathan Anderson has won this year's London Design Medal for his work "blending high fashion, art and craft".

While Anderson won the London Design Medal, the award scheme's highest accolade, Superflux co-founder Anab Jain was named winner of the Design Innovation Medal.

This year's Emerging Talent Medal was won by Mimica founder Solveiga Pakštaitė, while the Lifetime Achievement Medal awarded to academic Christopher Frayling.

The four design medals are awarded each year during London Design Festival (LDF), which starts this week.

"This year's medal winners demonstrate the transformative power of design, from Jonathan Anderson's work blending high fashion, art and craft, to Sir Christopher Frayling's lifelong dedication to design education and cultural history, Anab Jain's pioneering work in speculative futures, and Solveiga Pakštaitė's solutions for intuitive, inclusive and considered design," said LDF director Ben Evans.

"Each medal recipient exemplifies how creative innovation shapes our culture, industry and shared future."

Read:

"In these conditions, how can we be optimistic?" asks Anab Jain

A graduate of London College of Fashion, Anderson is best known for leading his own brand JW Anderson, and as creative director at fashion houses Loewe and Christian Dior.

"This award is incredibly special to me," said Anderson. "It is a true honour to be recognised by the LDF for my work within the field of craft and design, which have always been a personal passion of mine."

Jain, who co-founded Superflux with designer Jon Ardern, won the Emerging Talent Medal, which "recognises an individual or practice that has made a recent impact on the design scene and has an emerging practice showing design promise".

The studio was named Dezeen design studio of the year in 2021. It is know for its work weaving together technology, politics and culture.

"It is a real honour to receive the Design Innovation Medal," said Jain. "I share it with my Superflux co-founder Jon Ardern, and with everyone who has shaped the studio over the years.

"For us, it is recognition that speculative and future-led design is inherently innovative and entrepreneurial," she continued. "At Superflux, we have always believed that design’s greatest power lies in making complex, systemic futures viscerally felt, so people can step outside established narratives and find the courage to imagine alternate futures."

Frayling was awarded the Lifetime Achievement Medal to mark his long career in academia, including at the Royal College of Art where he established the History of Design masters course.

Alongside academia, Frayling has presented and written programmes for the BBC and Channel 4, as well as leading numerous institutions – including the Arts Council England, Design Council, Royal Mint Design Advisory Committee and Crafts Study Centre – as chairman.

Pakštaitė, who won this year's Emerging Talent Medal, founded tech food company Mimica. The brand gained international attention for Bump, a bio-reactive food label, which won the James Dyson Award in 2014.

More recently, she developed Looplets, an adaptable footwear system.

"I'm passionate about promoting inclusion and sustainable habits through design, and I think it's wonderful that work that makes the world a little bit better is being recognised," she said.

"I feel very honoured! I'm proud of what I have worked on so far but I'm even more excited by the design challenges yet to come."

Last year, designer Michael Anastassiades was awarded the London Design Medal, with architect Norman Foster receiving the lifetime achievement award.

The photography is courtesy of LDF.

item.content:encoded:
As Currents festival kicks off in Berlin, founders Laura Ewert and Jasmin Jouhar tell Dezeen why they hope the event will finally bring the local design community the recognition it deserves.

Running from today until 12 September, Currents was conceived as a "very Berlin" event – decentralised and community-curated, with minimal corporate sponsorship.

Much like Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design, it is funded almost entirely bottom-up by the brands and studios taking part.

"The concept is not really new, but it's also very Berlin," Ewert said. "We are used to creating something out of nothing. There is an empty room, then 10 people come together, and two weeks later there is a proper exhibition without much money."

"It's basically this spirit of DIYing," Jouhar added. "People in Berlin are not waiting for someone else to come and tell them: let's go do this now."

For the two journalists-turned-event organisers, the launch comes at a crucial time when there are more exciting studios and brands coming out of Berlin than ever, but scarce platforms and basically no funding for them to show off their work – either at home or abroad.

Several design festivals have attempted to represent the city over the years, most notably Berlin Design Week, which has been organised by branding studio State of Design since 2017. But the duo say these events have largely been shunned by the local community.

"The fact that there was no platform where Berlin designers felt comfortable showcasing their work always seemed a little odd, given the quality of design found here," Ewert explained.

Outside of Berlin, the picture doesn't look much rosier. Like many furniture fairs, Germany's longstanding IMM Cologne has struggled for attendance, cancelling its 2025 edition due to falling market demand, although it returned this year.

And while other major European economies are investing in spotlighting their talent on an international stage, the Currents organisers say German designers are largely left to fend for themselves.

"If you go to Milan [design week], you see Switzerland, you see Austria, and you see the effort and money they're putting in – we don't understand why Germany is not doing this," Ewert said. "We definitely want to change that."

Currents, too, was unable to procure public funding for the event, although not for lack of trying.

The duo suspect this largely comes down to the fact that, despite Germany's pedigreed design history, from the Bauhaus to Dieter Rams, appreciation for the discipline on a political and economic level is now largely a thing of the past.

"There was a crucial moment in post-war history where the German industry really was open to design," Jouhar said. "It was Braun with Dieter Rams and Erco with Otl Aicher. But this is over. The industry in Germany is no longer really open to what design can do for them, for their processes, for their products."

"In Germany, it's more about function than about design," Ewert agreed.

As a result, local designers are caught in a Catch-22 situation, where their work is undervalued by industry, yet ineligible for traditional arts or culture funding due to its commercial applications.

"The values of design that are cultural, social, political – they are not recognised," Ewert said. "And this is part of the problem, I would say. And that's one reason why funding is so tough."

Read:

FSB relaunches 1986 Dieter Rams door handle with "effortless grip"

In spite of all this, Berlin's design scene continues to flourish.

The city is now home to not just the odd household name like Konstantin Grcic or the Royal Porcelain Factory KPM, which dates back to 1763, but also to a growing cohort of exciting young studios and brands.

There's furnituremaker Objekte Unserer Tage, which is launching its Linde collection during Currents, and glass brand Moonarij, which works with local glass artisans, alongside buzzy independent firms like Llot Llov, Daftar and Hahn & Wolf.

In total, Currents will feature work from 80 brands and studios across 60 locations. And although some are from further afield, like German bathroom brand Kaldewei and Swedish flooring manufacturer Bolon, which just opened its first showroom in the city, the majority of the programme is dedicated to local Berliners.

The hope is that the event will finally drum up some much-needed recognition for a design scene that, Ewert says, has long been undervalued and underfunded.

"People are always asking, what has changed in the past few years," she explained. "When other events have failed, why are you doing this now?"

"I think one very important thing is that Berlin still has this DIY energy, but the stuff doesn't look DIY anymore. It's all on an international level. It's quality."

"When I compare it to what came out of Berlin like 15 years ago, it is much more professional," Jouhar agreed.

This is especially impressive, she argued, given that the city is so far removed from any large-scale manufacturing, following its deindustrialisation after the second world war.

"We don't have any industry in Berlin anymore," Jouhar explained. "All industry, but also the financial sector, all the real economy left for West Germany or other parts of Europe. So there is not this close connection to industry and production, like we have in Copenhagen or Milan."

As a result, the duo argue that Germany will always be slightly more decentralised than other European countries, with events like Munich Design Days and Cologne's Interior Design Days vying for international attention.

But despite its lack of industry connections, Ewert reckons Berlin has a real shot at establishing itself as Germany's new design capital. "We are getting there," she said.

"Let's start with Berlin," she added. "Our goal is to highlight the community and the good work that they are doing. And after we have done that and everyone sees that Berlin is still a very creative city and we have an extraordinary design scene, then we can think about all the other cities and countries."

Currents 2026 takes place from 10 to 12 September 2026 at various locations across Berlin, Germany. For other design events around the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower in London into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool for American hotelier MCR.

Orms will restore the Grade II-listed BT Tower, the adjacent podium and 1930s Howland Building, and convert the complex into a hotel with ground-floor shops, bars and restaurants, if the application is approved by the London Borough of Camden.

A publicly accessible swimming pool will be built on top of the podium, which will be overlooked by the iconic BT Tower structure.

Plans also include improving the public space around the building and opening the upper portion of the 177-metre-tall tower to the public for the first time since 1981.

"Our vision has always been to honour the BT Tower's remarkable history while reimagining its future," said MCR CEO Tyler Morse.

"Submitting our planning application is an exciting step towards reopening this landmark after almost 50 years, revitalising the area with new jobs and open space for Camden."

Read:

Richard and Su Roger's seminal house in London "gifted to the nation"

Originally designed by the Ministry of Public Building and Works, led by chief architects Eric Bedford and G R Yeats, the communications tower opened in 1964 as the Post Office Tower.

Designed to support microwave aerials, which were removed in 2011, the distinctive structure was topped by a revolving restaurant that closed in the early 1980s.

The BT Tower was the tallest building in London when it was built and retained the title until the NatWest Tower was built in 1980.

MCR first announced its acquisition of the tower in 2024. At the time, UK practice Heatherwick Studio was set to lead the transformation of the building into a hotel.

Orms took over the project earlier this year. Works are expected to commence in 2029, once the building has been fully vacated, and MCR plans for the transformation to be completed and open to the public by 2033.

Elsewhere in London, the seminal 22 Parkside house by Richard and Su Rogers was handed over from private ownership to the National Trust, and a group of 19th-century dinosaur sculptures at Crystal Palace Park were restored by HTA Design and Donald Insall Associates.

The images are by MCR, Orms and Secchi Smith.

item.content:encoded:
The British capital is bursting with emerging designers casting off convention and doing things their way. Ahead of London Design Festival, here are six names to have on your radar.

Tessa Silva

The stitcher: Tessa Silva started her career crafting vases from a clay-like material made from waste skimmed milk and chalk, which she developed over three years and fed through a sausage stuffer to create distinctive lumpy vessels. Asymmetric, swollen forms have been something of a throughline in Silva's constantly expanding portfolio ever since.

Her current focus is Smock, an ongoing project that involves smocking metres of fabric by hand to create intricately upholstered furniture pieces.

The collection includes a lounge chair made from hand-stitched horsehair and coconut fibres, which caused a stir when it appeared in the Max Radford Gallery presentation at this year's Collect show at Somerset House.

Silva is once again collaborating with the gallery during LDF as a contributor to its Progressive Permanence exhibition, which is taking place at the Christopher Farr showroom in Shoreditch.

Mitre & Mondays

The material geeks: Mitre & Mondays is the brainchild of Freya Bolton, Josef Shanley-Jackson and Finn Thomson, a trio on a simple mission to connect people to the material world around them.

Founded in 2019, the UK's answer to Formafantasma aims to investigate the broader implications of design, as well as the social and environmental impact of its production.

Mitre & Mondays sees design for disassembly at the centre of its practice, and for LDF has reconstructed its popular Wood for the Trees exhibition at the Shoreditch Tab Centre.

The studio is also responsible for the scenography of the Design Museum's new Mineral exhibition, made entirely from "reusable, reconfigurable or borrowed" materials – mostly stone offcuts from a Lincolnshire quarry.

Georgia Merritt

The trompe-l'œil painter: After finishing her degree in fine art at Goldsmiths in 2020 and struggling to find work, Georgia Merritt completed a gilding apprenticeship – an experience that armed her with a knack for the most granular of painting techniques.

As a designer, Merritt draws on this experience to create trompe l'œil faux marble furniture made of fibreboard, which she hand-paints and glazes to look like smooth, veiny stone.

The strength of Merritt's technique lies in her ability to use a more sustainable, low-cost wood-based product instead of actual stone, while maintaining a beautifully realistic marbled finish.

Ralph Parks

The self-taught carpenter: Ralph Parks has described the smoothed ashwood composition of his Rhine by Night standing cabinet as reminiscent of something fossilised or aged underwater over decades.

This poetic approach is typical of the designer, a self-taught carpenter with a penchant for inverting historic and religious motifs in his alternative timber pieces, including a curved armchair inspired by a Romanesque church.

Parks recently found an abandoned piece of unidentified wood and chipped away at it until he had produced a wall-mounted shelf with the undulating quality of an untreated tree branch, which was designed to hold keys or trinkets. His curiosity about what can be done with discarded timber shows no sign of slowing down.

Lewis Kemmenoe

The hardcore patchworker: Countless pieces of timber furniture have flooded the design world in recent years, but few craftspeople have managed to put such an instantly recognisable stamp on their creations as Lewis Kemmenoe.

The designer painstakingly collages slabs of wood together to achieve beautifully patchworked pieces, from neatly formed chairs to layered cabinets and bookshelves. He also applies the technique to metals including copper and aluminium, creating similar pieces of furniture that bear his quilt-like design language.

Barnaby Lewis

The blacksmith: Barnaby Lewis earned his stripes as a carpenter before realising he was far more drawn to working with steel. His back catalogue of collectible design has ranged from a gothic-style desk with spindly legs to room dividers adorned with abstract figures, moons and stars.

At this year's LDF, Lewis is presenting work in Brompton Design District as part of the second-ever Studio Iron show, the interdisciplinary design gallery set up by artist Isamaya Ffrench. When he's not conceiving intricate furniture, the blacksmith can be found patching up cars or solving whatever local steel-based puzzles he can get his hands on.

item.content:encoded:
During this year's London Design Festival, plywood furniture specialist Lozi will debut a modular system, including clean-lined wardrobes and a fold-down bed, that aims to offer an affordable alternative to bespoke cabinetry.

The idea for the collection emerged towards the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, when Lozi founder Soroush Pourhashemi received several requests from clients who needed their bedroom to also function as a workspace.

Bespoke solutions developed for this purpose can become prohibitively expensive, as they involve a great deal of costly and time-consuming design work and long manufacturing lead times.

Using his 14 years of experience creating custom-made furniture, Pourhashemi developed a series of pieces that can be used together to fully furnish a bedroom while offering the ease, convenience and lower cost of standalone furniture.

Pourhashemi told Dezeen that the solution allows users to "mix and match individual standalone units to create a freestanding piece that mimics fitted joinery, like how Ikea sells their iconic Billy Bookcase design."

The collection comprises three wardrobe designs, a fold-down Murphy bed, a desk unit, a chest of drawers and a freestanding bed frame, with optional bedside tables and a headboard.

Each piece can be easily adapted and combined with others to create a range of configurations without the need for bespoke design work.

"One of the biggest issues with small bedrooms is efficiently using the limited space," claimed Pourhashemi, pointing out that the units are available in a range of sizes starting at just 40 centimetres wide.

"Small bedrooms can also end up feeling very busy, so we kept all the designs very clean, with shelving and storage hidden behind beautifully finished doors rather than using open shelving."

The wardrobes include a unit with double doors, another with a single door and curved end sections that can be combined in various ways to fit any space.

The fold-down bed can also be used alongside the wardrobes to create a cohesive storage wall, with the bed disappearing when not in use.

Read:

POOR Collective's debut rug collection evokes London's Trellick Tower

Desk units can be used on their own or can slot in next to the wardrobes and bed, while the chest of drawers features a built-in vanity.

The standalone furniture was designed to complement the fitted units and includes an updated version of Lozi's best-selling curved bed frame, with a large storage drawer incorporated in the base.

The furniture is made at Lozi's Hackney Road workshop, using a custom-built modular jig system that enables all of the curved components to be fabricated using the same efficient process.

The brand's signature curved forms feature throughout the collection, adding style and personality to the pieces while reducing the risk of bumping into sharp edges when moving around a small space.

Pourhashemi founded Lozi in 2012 with the aim of creating furniture that is minimal and modern while displaying a distinct sense of personality.

The studio combines digital manufacturing and traditional woodworking methods to craft furniture that is mostly made to order, with the flexibility to adapt to custom measurements as well as offering a wide range of paint colours and veneer options.

The bedroom furniture collection is being launched in a range of four classic finishes – maple, oak, cherry and walnut – that showcase the wood's natural beauty and tactility.
