Promotion: Tile of Spain has announced its 2026 awards competition, inviting creatives to submit projects that spotlight the innovative use of Spanish ceramics.

The annual Tile of Spain Awards in Architecture and Interior Design champion the creative use of Spanish-made ceramic tiles in outstanding architecture and interior projects both in Spain and internationally.

The competition is open to architects, interior designers, landscape architects and decorators of any nationality.

Entrants may enter individually or as part of a team. There is a total prize fund of €35,000, which is split across different award categories, including Architecture and Interior Design.

Eligible projects must have been completed between January 2024 and October 2026 and must not have been submitted in previous editions of the awards.

Introduced last year, the awards now include subcategories within its Architecture and Interior Design categories.

Specifically, subcategories A-a and I-a are for projects using dry-pressed porcelain stoneware, while A-b and I-b are for projects using other ceramic materials, such as terracotta, rustic stoneware, glazed stoneware, extruded porcelain stoneware, wall tiles and mosaics.

This year's judging panel will be made up of professionals from the design industry, who are set to be announced later this year.

There are four prizes up for grabs, with €8,000 to be awarded across the professional Interior Design and Architecture categories. There is also a €3,000 prize for the Master's Thesis Project – a category dedicated to innovative student work.

The submission deadline is 22 October. Following this, the jury will meet in Castellón, Spain, to assess the entries and select the winning projects.

Last year's architecture prizes were awarded to Casa Marratxi by Casas inHAUS and Interventions in the Monastery of Santa María de Sijena by Pemán y Franco Arquitectos – Sebastián Arquitectos.

The top two prizes in the interior design category were awarded to Brickell Penthouse Miami by François Guglielmina – TOGU Miami Design, and Boc Beach by Il Mio design.

The awards are in their 25th year and are organised by the Spanish Ceramic Tile Manufacturers Association (ASCER). Tile of Spain encompasses more than 120 tile manufacturers and celebrates aesthetic and technical innovation in ceramic design.

Since 2004, Tile of Spain has supported a series of ceramic tile studies departments at different schools of architecture in Spain and abroad.

This year's awards are sponsored by Valenciaport and PwC Spain, with the support of the Conselleria de Economía, Hacienda y Administración Pública (Generalitat Valenciana).

To learn more about the competition and to download its entry form, visit its website.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: according to wallpaper specialist Selected Wallpapers, wallcoverings are increasingly equipped with woven, sound-absorbing and embossed qualities, which is changing "what a wall is asked to do".

Selected Wallpapers explained that there is an increasing demand for tactile wallpapers, which now play a large part in how a space looks and feels.

As interior design trends have shifted toward calmer, more restrained spaces, the brand added that wallpapers have become the chosen surface where texture and a room's personality are expressed.

"There is a moment, walking into a well-considered room, when you sense it before you can explain it," said Selected Wallpapers. "The light settles differently on the walls; the surfaces have depth; and almost without thinking, you want to run a hand along them."

"That instinct – to touch a wall rather than simply look at it – has quietly become one of the defining forces in contemporary luxury interiors," it continued.

The brand highlighted Abaca Métal by CMO Paris, which is made using abaca weft with a subtle metallic finish that responds to changing light.

Another example is Parthénon – Rayures Jumelles by Élitis, a three-dimensional textile wallcovering featuring raised linear and curved forms, which give it acoustic properties.

According to Selected Wallpapers, the shift towards incorporating tactile walls into design projects, from residential to commercial, is a response to increasing screen time and screens being placed at the centre of a room.

The brand explained that as daily life has become increasingly digital, the physical qualities of an interior – the warmth of a space and the way a surface catches light – carry "new emotional value".

For example, natural fibres, wood veneer and grass cloth absorb and reflect light, which "rewards closeness" as people move throughout a room at different times of the day.

It added that designers are also increasingly interested in "how a room sounds" and that many tactile surfaces are also designed to absorb sound reverberation, without a visible acoustic panel in sight.

"Designers increasingly talk about how a room feels and sounds, not only how it looks," the brand added.

An example is Soft Surrounds by Phillip Jeffries, which has a large-scale geometric pattern and a teddy-like fabric. It has sound-absorption qualities and is also stain-repellent, combining tactility with functional performance.

Another example is Vinacoustic Polyform Galeo by Texdecor, which is equipped with raised surfaces and textures.

The three-dimensional construction gives the material depth while also providing acoustic performance, illustrating how contemporary wallcoverings can "combine surface design with a functional role".

Selected Wallpapers represents 55 of the world's leading wallpaper houses and works with architects and interior designers across Europe.

The company are experts on tactile and acoustic collections and advises architects on the right weave and fibre for a particular light, room and acoustics. The team also advises on how a surface will age.

item.content:encoded:
Technology company Apple has released its first folding smartphone that has the largest screen of any iPhone.

Called iPhone Duo, the phone is the first folding-screen device in Apple's product lineup. It features a central hinge mechanism as well as an external screen visible when the device is folded.

"[iPhone Duo] redefines the experience of using a foldable phone," said Apple CEO John Ternus during a Wednesday virtual presentation.

It marks the entry of the company into the foldable screen market. It is the first major change in the phone's form since Apple released its first touchscreen phones in 2007.

Apple vice president of industrial design Molly Anderson said that the phone, when folded, is around the same size as a passport. When folded, it measures 5.4 inches long with about 90 per cent of the aspect ratio of the iPhone 18 Pro, also announced today.

Anderson added that the phone is the "largest iPhone display ever designed" when unfolded at 7.6 inches. It has a titanium enclosure and "ceramic shields" on the front and back of the shell.

The screen also allows the front-facing camera to be covered by the display.

It features a central hinge with a "variable torque profile" and over 100 components so that the device can sit partially open. It can be used in this semi-open state, held like a book or placed on a surface like a laptop computer.

The screen component has multi-layered lamination with scratch-resistant glass on the top.

It has speakers on two sides, and the external and internal screens have the same aspect ratio.

Two external cameras were integrated with the company's upgraded aperture features.

Read:

Apple launches first-ever budget MacBook

The company also released custom cases for the product, one with a "kickstand".

Ternus said that the foldable phone was the best way to make the iPhone an "intelligent personal hub".

Apple announced updates to its other products, including the iPhone 18, set to release next year, as well as a new edition of the Apple Watch.

It also updated its vapour chamber cooling systems, integrating recycled steel and a copper plate.

The release comes nearly 20 years after Apple first released the iPhone in 2007 under then-design officer Jony Ive.

The folding OLED-screen phone has been tried by a number of other companies. Samsung's Galaxy Fold was released in 2019. Last year, Chinese company Honor released a folding phone that it claims is the "world's thinnest".

The images are courtesy of Apple.

Dezeen Showroom: Italian tile brand Casalgrande Padana has advertised a selection of its latest tiles on Dezeen Showroom, showing the varied and expressive potential of porcelain stoneware.

Among the designs is the company's Saxum outdoor tiles, which, like the rest of the Saxum line, celebrate the beauty of natural stone.

These tiles feature elegant veining across their mineral-like surface and come in five elegant, sandy shades.

The outdoor tiles have a thickness of 20 millimetres and an anti-slip Grip surface, and can be either laid on screed for high load resistance or dry laid on sand, gravel or turf to make an instant path.

Casalgrande Padana's Essence line is another that channels the beauty of natural materials, this time honing in on larch wood with its warm character and rich grain.

These tiles have a realistic surface created through Casalgrande Padana's advanced technologies and form part of the brand's Elements collection, which brings together three complementary styles for harmoniously mix-and-matched layouts.

The Essence range comes in six shades and includes a decorative option called Essence Cannetté, combining the same wood effect with a slatted-look 3D surface.

This tile brings sophisticated layered texture into interiors and looks particularly striking on feature walls, kitchen islands and other vertical surfaces.

For even more personality, there is Imagina Abstract, a new range of decorative tiles designed to be close to works of art. Bold abstract designs feature heavily in the collection, ranging from bright pinstripe-like lines to delicate metallic inlays and large-scale murals.

The Klimt design evokes a massive painted canvas, while Inlay creates a trompe l'oeil effect with its architectural composition of angles and gradients.

The Imagina line also includes designs that put a modern twist on florals with Imagina Floral, either blowing them up to a contemporary large scale or obscuring them in mists.

Windflower features layers of delicate gold and grey leaves as if in a meadow dreamscape, while Florilege evokes classic elegance with its spread of white flowers on a black background.

Founded in 1960 and manufacturing entirely in Italy, Casalgrande Padana is known for its high-performance porcelain stoneware.

It has consistently pushed the technologies of tile manufacturing, with advances such as Bios Antibacterial, which removes up to 99.99 per cent of common household bacterial strains.

item.content:encoded:
With the professional American football season kicking off today, we take a look at some upcoming stadiums and overhauls, from Washington DC to Kansas City.

Late this summer, global architecture studio Populous completed a ground-up stadium for the Buffalo Bills in New York, representing a new wave in NFL stadium construction in the East.

The last major wave of stadiums for the league happened in the early 2020s with SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles and Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, both built to accommodate teams moving into the cities.

In the late 2020s and early 2030s, a new generation of NFL stadiums will come online. Two of the stadiums included in this list are new builds, while the other two are overhauls of existing structures. In the design, we see a trend towards enclosed stadiums with glass roofs and plenty of auxiliary development.

Two stadiums not included are the upcoming Bears stadium, as the team is still figuring out whether it will leave Chicago, and the Broncos stadium in Denver, which has a master plan and architect but no renderings as of yet.

Read on for the next generation of NFL stadiums.

Everbank Stadium, Florida, by HOK, 2028

Instead of building a new stadium, the Jacksonville Jaguars have opted to wrap their current stadium in a new expressive facade complete with mirrored elements and LED screens, a massive departure from the current steel-framed, open-bowl stadium.

Designed in 1996 by HOK Sport (now Populous), the current stadium is open to the elements, which presents challenges in the wet, hot climate of Jacksonville.

HOK has dubbed its design for the 62,000-seat venue as the "Stadium of the Future".

It will have openings on the outside to help modulate the temperature and feature an overhang above the stands, as well as extensive landscaping on the perimeter, which has been described as a "subtropical" park.

Find out more about Everbank Stadium ›

Commanders Stadium at RFK Campus, Washington DC, by HKS, 2030

No other stadium in recent memory has caused as much of a stir as the upcoming 70,000-seat stadium for the Washington Commanders – except for maybe the drama over the Bears' potential move to Indiana.

Due to its proximity to the national capital, the federal government has put its hand on the scale of the design, with a Trump aide publically calling for the stadium to be collonaded, in line with the government's classical architecture mandates.

The HKS-designed result walks the line between the classical and the modern, with a plinth, columns and an elegant cable-net, anti-clastic glass roof framing views of the Capitol building and other landmarks.

Located next to the Anacostia River on the site of the former RFK Stadium, the building will feature extensive outbuildings in hopes of fostering a stadium district, as well as hardscaping for pregames and other civic uses.

Find out more about Commanders Stadium at RFK Campus ›

Bank of America Stadium, North Carolina, by HOK, 2030

Much like in Jacksonville, HOK will return to renovate a stadium completed by HOK Sport in the late 1990s for the Carolina Panthers in Charlotte.

The renovation here will take a lighter approach than in Jacksonville, though, and the new Bank of America Stadium is only one featured here without the glass roof structure, with the Panthers preferring to keep the structure open.

A new crown will be added to the top of the stadium, which the team said will resemble a crown, a not-so-subtle reference to Charlotte's moniker – "Queen City".

The base of the structure will be clad in glass while the "strategic interventions" will add plazas and park-like space to the exterior.

Find out more about Bank of America Stadium ›

Chiefs Stadium, Kansas, by Manica and HTNB, 2031

Careful readers may notice that the above says Kansas and not Missouri, the side of the two-state city where the Kansas City Chiefs have played at Arrowhead Stadium for more than 50 years.

The new 70,000-seat structure was designed to pay homage to Arrowhead Stadium with red facade elements that slope up dramatically.

However, the new stadium will feature a glass-covered roof with an anti-clastic roof similar to the design for Commanders Stadium.

Notably, the stadium will eschew the sports district, connected model and be located relatively far from the urban core and surrounded by parking lots, which the studio said will be specifically tailored to tailgating.

Find out more about Chiefs Stadium ›

An evolution of the 15-year-old TNK500 task chair, the TNK500 Aurea is designed for workplaces that prioritise both ergonomics and aesthetics.

item.content:encoded:
A metal tunnel guides visitors from underground into a lofty exhibition hall within a tram depot at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, which was designed by French architecture practice Studio KO in Uzbekistan's capital.

Commissioned by the chair of Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF), Gayane Umerova, the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent) was designed as a landmark to amplify the city's cultural visibility.

CCA Tashkent spans two ornamental yellow-brick buildings, designed in 1912 by architect Wilhelm Heinzelmann. One was an administration building, and the other was a tram depot and diesel station, where residual oily scents still permeate its brick walls.

Studio KO designed the heart of the project in the tall, industrial hall of the diesel station, which is lined with high-level windows and its original brick walls.

The team compared this space to a cathedral, or its own version of the Turbine Hall at London's Tate Modern.

"It was already very monumental, almost like a basilica with its proportions," Studio KO director Olivier Marty told Dezeen on a tour of the building. "We remained very faithful to it."

Now open to the public, CCA Tashkent will serve as a hub for cultural exhibitions, education and research.

Visitors enter from the old administration building, which has been converted into a reception, gift shop and offices for staff. On its top level is a skylit library with a snug for listening to records.

The shell of this building was transformed and expanded through the insertion of a blocky, self-supporting volume, which appears to swell out from the old brick structure, breaking open one of its corners.

This new geometric volume deliberately contrasts with the existing fabric, cloaked with chunky gravel used locally to mix concrete, and finished with a glossy varnish.

From the reception, a statement helical staircase winds down below ground into the first gallery space, described by Marty as an "anteroom" to the main space. From here, visitors are guided through a dark metal-lined tunnel that opens into the basement of the diesel station.

This area contains a second exhibition area, alongside bleacher-like seating that doubles as a staircase to the main hall, running beneath a cubic auditorium suspended overhead.

This sequence leads from a dark, low-lying space into the bright, spacious main hall, creating an unexpected shift in atmosphere that emphasises the room's stateliness.

Above, the technical services are left exposed, accentuating the hall's industrial feel.

"This area is interesting as it is where you understand the monumentality of [the main hall]," Marty reflected.

"The other spaces obviously have their own sort of scenery, but this space is comparable to something like the Turbine Hall – a slightly smaller version – and that was intended," added chief curator Sara Raza.

Material contrasts feature throughout the project, with steely metal panels lining the auditorium walls and the tunnel, creating a juxtaposition with the original brickwork.

Several wooden details add warmth, complemented by dark and earthy terrazzo that envelops several walls and floors as an homage to Soviet-era modernism, according to Marty.

"The contemporary interventions are designed to be legible as an extreme contrast with the existing fabric of the building," explained the architect.

The large windows lining the building are coated with a purple-coloured filter, which is only visible from the outside.

At the end of the journey through the structures, visitors are guided out to a large open-air courtyard that serves as an additional exhibition space.

It is hugged by sweeping walls, also finished in the dark, shiny gravel, which frame a restaurant, an adaptable workshop space for children and a prayer room.

Read:

Lina Ghotmeh set to turn historic Uzbeki house into Jadids' Legacy Museum

According to Marty, the courtyard is modelled on a "contemporary version of a traditional mahala" – a traditional type of residential Uzbek neighbourhood arranged around courtyards.

This was an effort to establish the outdoor area as its own space, which reads as separate from the buildings without competing or feeling secondary to them.

"It was very hard to imagine a courtyard between those two very strong buildings," he explained. "We didn't want to mimic the bricks, we needed to be honest in the modern edition and to create something that doesn't compete with it."

The building has opened with an exhibition titled Hikmah, curated by Raza, showcasing works by 10 artists. The furniture used throughout is a bespoke set of modular metal-and-wooden pieces designed by Studio KO.

Other major architecture projects underway in Uzbekistan include Lina Gotmeh's transformation of a historic home in Bukhara into the Jadids' Legacy Museum and Tadao Ando's National Museum of Uzbekistan in Tashkent.

In July, 10 of Tashkent's key modernist buildings were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites, making them some of the youngest structures on the list.

item.content:encoded:
The modernist 22 Parkside house in Wimbledon, London, by Richard and Su Rogers has been given over to conservation charity The National Trust.

Designed by the pair in the late 1960s for Richard Rogers' parents, ownership of 22 Parkside has passed from the Rogers family to The National Trust, which plans to host events and guided tours of the seminal house.

Opening to the public on Saturday as part of London's Open House festival, the house is a celebrated example of modernist architecture and considered to be a prototype for Richard Rogers' later works, including the Lloyd's of London building and the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Conservation group Twentieth Century Society celebrated the passing of ownership to The National Trust, hoping that it will ensure the long-lasting future of 22 Parkside.

Read:

22 Parkside "led to most of the work I do" says Richard Rogers

"The Society is thrilled to see this Grade II*-listed modernist masterpiece of 20th-century architecture gifted to the nation," said Twentieth Century Society director Catherine Croft. "We can think of no better custodians than the National Trust to safeguard its future."

"With structural steel portal frames more commonly found in industrial buildings, windows from a bus, and insulation panels from a refrigerated truck, it's a prefabricated prototype for modern living unlike almost any other home in Britain," she continued.

"From this small acid-yellow pavilion off Wimbledon Common, to the heights of the Pompidou Centre and the Lloyd's Building, the house paved the way for the globe-straddling avant-garde architecture that followed."

The single-storey home is constructed from a yellow-painted steel frame with glass facades, designed to demonstrate how pre-fabrication could enable homes to be built quickly and affordably.

"22 Parkside is much more than a family home," said Ben Rogers, son of Richard and Su Rogers. "It is one of the most important buildings my father and mother created – a place where many of the ideas that would go on to influence my father's work and some of the world's most celebrated architecture were first tested and explored."

"As a family, we wanted to ensure that this remarkable house would be protected, cared for and shared with future generations, rather than remaining a private asset," he continued. "The National Trust brings the expertise, public purpose and long-term commitment needed to safeguard its future, while opening up its story to students, researchers and visitors."

Pritzker Prize-winning architect and high-tech pioneer Richard Rogers died in 2021 aged 88. In 2013, Dezeen interviewed the influential architect about his work on 22 Parkside, in which he revealed the house "led to most of the work I do".

The photography is by Megan Taylor

item.content:encoded:
A clutch of young design galleries and grassroots platforms are shaking the cobwebs off London's design scene. In the lead-up to the city's annual design festival, we profile five that you should know about.

Design Everything

The collective: after being quoted £900 per square metre to show in an emerging design show at LDF 2024, London designer Lewis Duckworth decided to throw his own. Joined by Tabatha Pearce Chedier, Jacob Marks, Eleanor Murphy and Sammi Cherryman, the effort to organise these free shows quickly turned collective.

"We're all kind of co-parenting Design Everything," joked Duckworth.

Following the guerrilla exhibition they hosted out of the back of a van in 2025, their annual presentation has gone mainstream this year with a zero-fee, open-call show at design shop Aram, featuring work from no fewer than 100 designers.

Outside of LDF, the collective also runs regular meet-ups and has turned its website into an emerging designer directory to keep the community alive throughout the year.

Online and at Aram for LDF

Unit.d

The actually affordable one: although it's been less than six months since Unit.d opened in a glorified garage near Haggerston station, the gallery has quietly revolutionised London's design scene.

Counter to the collectible design hegemony, its speciality lies in well-made, mass-produced everyday objects: wall hooks, bottle openers, etc. Despite being made by the likes of Jasper Morrison, Michael Marriott and Alexandra Gerber, the pieces are universally affordable, with most retailing for under £50.

Unit.d's monthly shows have also offered the community a much-needed chance to congregate regularly, likened by some to a "church service affair" – but with beer (more on that later).

Unit.d isn't showing at LDF this year, although founder Duncan Riches already has plans to take the gallery to Milan for next year's Salone del Mobile.

4 Frederick Terrace, E8 4EW, and online

Slancha

The Scottish export: Slancha was born in 2022 to address the lack of spaces for emerging designers in Scotland, including founders Harvey Everson and Findlay MacDonald, to show and sell their work.

With the young Scottish design scene finally gathering steam thanks to platforms such as theirs, the duo has moved down south, aiming to bring underrepresented talent from across Britain and Northern Ireland to London's global stage.

"We want to cover as much of the UK as possible," explained Everson.

After making its LDF debut in 2025, Slancha returns this year with not one but three different shows: two at The Hoxton hotel and another at concept store Awaykin.

Online and at The Hoxton and Awaykin for LDF

Max Radford Gallery

The next-gen blue chip: at its new HQ on Vyner Street, Max Radford Gallery is representing some of the buzziest names in London's collectible design scene: Andu Masebo, Lewis Kemmenoe and Tessa Silva.

From the get-go in 2020, its mission was to fill the gap left by established galleries reluctant to take a bet on a new generation of talent.

Six years on, the gallery faces a juggling act of continuing to push its roster of rising stars to new heights while also lifting up new voices.

"It's about balance," said founder Max Radford, "because you don't want to become one of the blue chips where you just work with a stable of five people for the next 20 years."

25 Vyner Street, E29DG, and at Christopher Farr for LDF

Allotment

The incubator: the brains behind birdwatching collective Flock Together, Ollie Olanipekun, turned the ground floor of his Haggerston office into an experimental gallery last year. Allotment gives local designers, artists and recent graduates a place to exhibit for free before taking it to commercial galleries.

"We're very much an incubator space," said Olanipekun.

As the name suggests, the aim is to spotlight work that connects nature and culture, with a recent show inviting attendees to build their own bio-fabricated lamp.

Soon, the gallery is set to move into a Hackney nature reserve, where a space has already been earmarked, to place the work in more direct dialogue with the environment.

Unit 8 Ability Plaza, Arbutus Street, E8 4DT

item.content:encoded:
Design gallery Béton Brut has teamed up with manufacturer Isokon to reinterpret Marcel Breuer's plywood furniture for the company, showcasing it "in a new way" with the Masur Edition at London Design Festival.

The collection is launching at London Design Festival (LDF) in time for the 90th anniversary of Breuer's original 1930s designs for Isokon, and will be on display in Béton Brut's east London showroom.

Breuer's original furniture designs for Isokon were made from plywood, but could also be finished with other woods such as sycamore, zebrano, mahogany and Australian walnut.

Called Masur Edition, the new collection aims to challenge the idea that the Breuer pieces were always made from plywood and intended to remain unadorned.

"Historical examples produced during his time as chief designer at Isokon featured a range of finishes, demonstrating plywood's capacity for material variation and expression," Béton Brut founder Sophie Pearce told Dezeen.

The Masur Edition comprises four Breuer designs – the Cut-Out Armchair, Cut-Out Chair, Isokon Nesting Tables and Isokon Dining Table, all of which were designed in 1936.

The pieces all have Isokon's signature clean, simple shapes, but have been updated with decoratively patterned masur birch.  The wood, which is grown in northern Europe, is rare and features distinctive swirls and small knots caused by fungal or bacterial activity.

"Chosen for its elusive, graphic character, masur birch introduces a psychedelic quality to Breuer's precise modernist forms," Pearce said.

"Its intricate figuring creates a striking contrast with the clarity and restraint of the designs, giving a different feel to these familiar works – all while remaining faithful to Breuer's vision."

Read:

Fourteen must-see exhibitions and installations at London Design Festival 2026

The Masur Edition will be a limited-edition launch, with prices starting at £1,300 and no set number of pieces.

"Masur veneer is scarce and difficult to source in high volume," Pearce explained. "The works will be sold exclusively through the gallery on a made-to-order basis, with a lead time of approximately 10 to 12 weeks."

Béton Brut has sold a number of early Isokon pieces over the years, Pearce said, which has created a connection between the gallery and Isokon's work. To her, working with Breuer's designs and reinterpreting them for today's world was both daunting and exciting.

"There's a responsibility that comes with working with such iconic pieces, but it's also exciting to showcase them in a new way whilst staying true to the ethos of Béton Brut gallery, which is to present limited bodies of exclusive works," Pearce said.

"Being able to contribute in some small way to the story of Isokon and Marcel Breuer has been a real privilege."

Other product launches during LDF include a rug collection that evokes London's Trellick Tower. We have also collected 14 unmissable events and exhibitions to visit during the design week.

The photography is by Ben Anders.

Masur Editions is on show at Béton Brut, Unit 2, 30 Felstead Street, London, from 12 to 20 September 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
A red travertine kitchen and a dark dining room with rounded timber walls form the heart of this home in East Sussex by Irish interiors firm Anam Design Studio.

Anam Design Studio overhauled the home interior with tactile stone surfaces and deep tones of wood and ceramic tiles, aiming to create a warm and inviting setting that suited the client's love of craft.

"We endeavour to use natural materials such as timber and stone in all our designs," Anam Design Studio director Liz Hughes told Dezeen. "We feel that as humans we are more akin to natural finishes in our environment and we also believe that they age better than man-made materials."

"We find ourselves increasingly drawn to these materials in an age of technology and social media noise," she continued.

The kitchen was designed to be the heart of the home, with slabs of red travertine forming a kitchen island and countertops that wrap around the walls into a window bench.

Bespoke dark oak cabinets and metallic accents add to the warm tones of the kitchen, and an existing black aga was re-enamelled in brown and bronze to fit the colour scheme.

Adjacent to the kitchen is a round dining room that Hughes described as "the most exciting but challenging part of the design".

"The dining room had very little natural light, so we embraced this area by giving it the feel of a bar or club," she said.

Read:

DAB Studio lines kitchen of Dutch home with oak and Afromosia wood

Two stone-lined openings puncture the curved oak walls on opposite sides of the dining room, which also has a hidden curved door leading to the lobby.

Upholstered seating, shelving, and a stone-and-lacquer table were custom-made to fit the circular space, and a large rounded ceiling light illuminates the room from above.

Elsewhere in the home are two connected reception spaces. The front room has a light and airy feel, while the adjacent reception and TV room has a deeper colour palette with lacquer-finished oak panels adorning the walls.

Anam Design Studio added a stone surround to the opening between the light and dark rooms, aiming to highlight the difference between the spaces.

"The front reception is south-facing and has plenty of natural light," said Hughes. "In the rear reception we went moodier, as it was a place for quiet contemplation or nighttime entertainment."

"We wanted to punctuate the opening between the two contrasting rooms," said Hughes. "In the rear reception, the stone [surround] marries beautifully with the dark timber panelling. In the front section, it contrasts with the off-white walls and complements the dark cardosa stone fireplace."

A similar mix of dark oak and stone surfaces was applied to the bedrooms and study, with natural wool and linen fabrics designed to add to the tactility of the interiors.

A red-tiled bathroom in the home features a coordinating Rosso Levanto marble basin, and a green-tiled bathroom is complemented with Verde Alpi marble flooring.

Other home interiors that used a rich mix of stone and wood include a family home in the Netherlands by DAB Studio and an energy-saving home in London by Architecture for London.

The photography is by Daniëlle Siobhán.

item.content:encoded:
A shading system comprised of copper-coloured ovals was added to the 205 North Quay tower in Brisbane, Australia, to combat the harsh subtropical sun.

Created by Australian studios Hassell and Richards & Spence, as well as American studio REX, the 30-storey office tower was informed by traditional Queenslander homes and designed to respond to local climate conditions.

The studios added shades to its facade to reduce the harsh sunlight and the heat, while plants, verandahs, terraces and outdoor spaces aim to create workplace wellbeing.

Located along the north bank of Brisbane River, the building core was positioned on its north side to free up the space close to the river, creating views of the river and of a cultural district located on its south bank.

Copper-coloured ellipse-shaped shades, which the studios say use less material than a traditional shading system, were added to the two longer facade elevations on the east and west sides of the tower.

The sunshades reduce the sun's impact while still providing natural light and clear views. According to the studios, the breathable facade also enables natural ventilation and reduces the building's overall energy use.

"205 North Quay asserts its commercial value not by wilful form, but by shrink-wrapping a slender, highly efficient structure in an equally efficient, state-of-the-art enclosure tailored to Brisbane's subtropical climate," said Joshua Ramus, founding principal from REX.

"Both its core and shell are designed to intensify the building's simplicity, office diversity, and ultra-transparency: the extraordinary sense of floating above the Brisbane River," he continued.

Read:

World's tallest timber tower tops out in Sydney

Each floor features a landscaped outdoor terrace on the east facade, creating an open gap at the centre of the otherwise sunshade-covered exterior.

205 North Quay also has a shaded open-air plaza at its street level that is accessible to both office workers in the building and the general public.

The building also has an outdoor rooftop terrace, as well as a dedicated wellness floor with a 25-metre lap pool and a gym.

"Our goal was to design a building that works with Brisbane's subtropical climate," Hassell principal Liam Short said. "By using shading, natural ventilation, and layered outdoor spaces, we've reduced energy demand while creating a healthier, more comfortable workplace."

Elsewhere in Australia, the world's tallest timber tower has topped out in Sydney, while Billard Leece Partnership has designed a children's hospital in Sydney with folded metal facade.

item.content:encoded:
Danish furniture brand OMHU has released a version of its Teddy sofa bed on third-party websites for a fraction of its usual price to draw attention to copy culture and to work as marketing.

Last weekend, the company released its own limited-edition "dupe" of the Teddy sofa. Intentionally misspelling the name and lowering the price, the brand said it wanted to bring awareness to what it views as the problem of dupes.

According to OMHU, the project is based on market research conducted after its original Teddy sofa went viral in 2022. The research established dupes sold online, and not other brands, as its biggest competitors.

"The OMHU Teddy is one of the most duped pieces of furniture out there, which is quite the compliment, but a tiring issue nonetheless," OMHU creative director Christine Smith told Dezeen.

"Normally you'd just report dupes or ignore them, but we spotted a creative opportunity to turn the issue on its head and build some global awareness around the real cost of buying cheap."

"We decided to make fun of the competition by beating them at their own game: misspelt name, selling on dupe retailers and all, while still proving a point that we're the OG of sofas".

The Tedy is a replica of the original Teddy sofa, a two-seater sofa upholstered in 90 per cent polyester, with a chrome-plated steel frame. The sofa is also modular and expands into a bed or large floor cushion.

The Tedy is made with the same materials and construction as the Teddy but upholstered in a bright "dupe-orange". It retails for $799.99 as opposed to the Teddy, which retails at $1,995.

OMHU said it set the cost based on the average price of dupes online, and sold 50 of the limited-edition sofas on websites such as Temu, Etsy and Dupe.com instead of its own website.

Instead of "pointing fingers", OMHU wanted to "outdupe them".

Read:

Planned London Design Festival installation "extremely close to my earlier projects" says Yuri Suzuki

The strategy is to meet audiences where they would normally shop for more affordable versions, according to the brand, though it's unclear how this might affect future business practices or pricing.

The 50 Tedys were released on 5 September and sold out within 10 minutes, according to OMHU.

The brand has spun out a whole marketing campaign on top of the release, including hiring lookalike influencers and hosting look alike competitions.

"The concept didn't stop with the sofa," said the brand.

"OMHU made dupe culture the entire marketing strategy, creating 'dupefluencers' – celebrity lookalike influencers recruited to launch their lookalike sofa."

"OMHU turned the trend into its own spin on influencer marketing."

Though the pattern of knock-offs is not new one, OMHU also pointed out a growth in dupe culture in connection to Gen Z and internet culture, noting the trend's expansion from fashion into furniture and design.

"Every iconic brand goes through this," said OMHU CEO Simon Salomonsson. "This isn't just our fight. We welcome any brand that is tired of being copied to join the conversation."

Dupes and copying are an ongoing issue in the design world. Emeco recently sued Zara Home for allegedly copying and selling a chair designed by Norman Foster and technology company Digby partnered with Heller on a tool that examined the authenticity of physical design products using NFTs in 2023.

The photography is courtesy of OMHU.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios Populous and Moody Nolan have released designs for a professional basketball and hockey arena based on the shape of Philadelphia's iconic Spectrum arena.

The planned arena will serve as the home of NBA team the 76ers and the NHL team the Flyers, as well as a forthcoming WNBA team.

The planned venue will replace the Xfinity Mobile Arena, which was completed in 1996 in the South Philadelphia Sports Complex, where the city's NFL stadium is also located.

Populous and Moody Nolan designed a circular structure with concentric stacked rings. The rings, which will be slightly offset, will alternate between glazed facades and LED displays.

The teams said that the design was based on the Spectrum, an arena built in 1967 and designed by SOM that was demolished in 2011.

"The new arena will connect the next gathering place for Philadelphia sports and entertainment to one of the city's most storied sports sites for future generations," said a press release from the Flyers and 76ers.

"The arena's architecture draws inspiration from the shape of the Spectrum, which hosted the Flyers and the 76ers for nearly three decades, and reimagines it through a contemporary design lens," continued the statement.

"The exterior will be defined by stacked, cantilevered bands that break down the scale of a typical arena and create a bold, instantly recognizable profile as a new South Philadelphia landmark."

Read:

Populous designs Charlotte Hornets facility clad in "swarm" of panels

The plaza around the stadium will be dedicated to "active outdoor spaces" and the teams compared the entry stairs to other Philadelphia landmarks such as its art museum.

There will be restaurants on the half-acre of outdoor space, with the final form still pending fan feedback.

According to the joint statement from the 76ers' and Flyers' owners, Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment and Comcast Spectacor, respectively, the project is set to be the "largest fully privately funded project in the city's history".

Course: Masterstudio Design
Tutors: Nicole Schneider, Andreas Wenger, Shehrie Islamaj, Jacqueline Loekito and Daniel Harris

School statement:

"The Masterstudio Design at the Institute Contemporary Design Practices (ICDP) is composed of three studios: Masterstudio Industrial Design, Masterstudio Scenography and Masterstudio Fashion Design.

"Each studio has a disciplinary focus. In addition, the research discourse of the ICDP focuses on Digital Integration, Design Cultures and Circular Design and are reflected and communicated multidimensionally.

"The basis of our applied research and project work is the design term 'advanced design'.

"Instead of the current economic practice of maximisation, we adopt the role of the extrapreneur in teaching and design, which stands for collaboration and systemic action.

"Current issues on global crises, climate change and social inequality are discussed and further developed.

"Sustainability and ecology, inclusion and technology, interaction and materiality are the fields in which the role of design is questioned and new visions for human coexistence and economic activity are defined.

"The Masterstudio Design offers in-depth training in professional, future-oriented design practice and applied research.

"Relevant research questions are identified and defined, appropriate and complex design processes are conceived, projects are developed and implemented.

"Communication, project management, cross-disciplinary and research-oriented teamwork are components of the training."

Etwas ist geblieben – Fabers Kammer by Alexander Prekas

"Drawing on theoretical research and interviews with artists, I examine how narrative spaces create sensory experiences, shift perspectives and offer temporary detachment from digital life.

"Building on these findings, I developed etwas ist geblieben – Fabers Kammer, an immersive narrative space inspired by Fahrenheit 451.

"Through a 1:1 installation, visitors enter Faber's chamber, explore objects, sounds, and smells, and gradually reconstruct his story.

"The work addresses censorship, digital desensitisation, and the need for conscious, sensory experiences."

Student: Alexander Prekas
Course: Studio Scenography
Mentors: Andreas Wegener, Martina Ehleiter and Ruth Scheel

Triggering Ritual: Ceramic as a Multisensory Design Medium by Boyun Choi

"Ceramic defines the modern bathroom yet remains largely unnoticed.

"This research investigates why ceramic has become invisible despite its presence and explores its potential as a multisensory design medium for ritual self-care.

"Drawing on multisensory perception, embodied memory and ritual formation, the study examines ceramics' tactile, acoustic and visual qualities.

"A survey of 60 participants, alongside interviews with two specialists at Laufen, reveals a gap between ceramics' sensory potential and its current use.

"The research identifies three conditions for ceramic to trigger ritual: sensory presence, consistency and intentionality, reframing the bathroom as a space where material, body and habit converge."

Student: Boyun Choi
Course: Studio Industrial Design
Tutors: Nicole Schneider, Werner Baumhakl, Pia Scharf and Naïma Trabelsi

The Center of Her World by Bruna Ideias

"A modular furniture system for the birthing room, currently in development.

"My project challenges the delivery bed as the default centrepiece of the maternity ward, a form that signals rest and passivity regardless of position, even when builtfor multiple postures.

"Working with two midwives, I am exploring how warm tones, soft curves and natural materials could prime the body for movement and verticality, replacing scattered aids like the solitary birthing ball or stool.

"Rather than proposing one object, my goal is to offer a platform for autonomy, making the birthing person, not the bed, the centre of the room."

Student: Bruna Ideias
Course: Studio Industrial Design
Tutor: Nicole Schneider

Plant Intimacies by Elisa Bartat

"This thesis examines how natural history museums display nature and how scenographic practices can reinforce anthropocentric narratives.

"Drawing on ecological relationality and more-than-human theories, it investigates how exhibition spaces shape knowledge and frame relationships between humans and the natural world.

"The research identifies anthropocentrism as a systemic condition within museum display, situated between control and care.

"In response, Plant Intimacies proposes an open, living installation that dissolves the vitrine and brings plants and people together.

"Plants are presented not as objects, but as relational agents, offering an intimate way to experience ecological belonging through sensory encounter."

Student: Elisa Bartat
Course: Studio Scenography
Tutors: Charlotte Tamschick, Martina Ehleiter and Ruth Scheel

Valere by Elvira Grau

"This collection explores value and appreciation through fashion as a multisensory experience that fosters emotional connection and empowerment.

"Inspired by daily life, nature and life cycles, it presents fashion as an expressive language.

"The work combines sculptural silhouettes, hand-painted silk prints, and detailed craftsmanship, with a special focus on footwear design and the transformation of existing shoes.

"Traditional St Gallen embroidery connects Swiss textile heritage with contemporary design.

"Conceived from head to toe, the looks create immersive silhouettes that unite individuality, preciousness and contemporary storytelling."

Student: Elvira Grau
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutors: Priska Morger, Jörg Wiese and Ruth Scheel

Fragments of Waldenburg by Lia Schürpf

"This project was developed in collaboration with Kaserne Basel and the Masterstudio Scenography (FHNW).

"For the site-specific parcours Waldenburg (12-14 June 2026), I created four participatory scenographic installations.

"They invite residents and visitors to actively shape the experience before, during, and after the parcours.

"Drawing on Waldenburg's existing visual landscape, the works transform familiar elements and reveal them in new contexts, encouraging audiences to experience the place from a fresh perspective."

Student: Lia Schürpf
Course: Studio Scenography
Tutors: Andreas Wenger and Martina Ehleiter

MDK by Miranda Kistler

"With a mixed cultural background and a background in photography and art, I wondered what we hold on to deeply when in constant flux?

"Every object is a vessel for a memory we fear losing. Yet, constant shift transforms us into curators of our lives.

"We learn the profound act of intentional loss, leaving valuable fragments in specific places as anchors, as reminders of where we root our sense of home and a promise that we will eventually return.

"My design practice is born from this fluid existence. Designing with intention and functionality, creating work that is not only rooted in change but explicitly meant to be changed.

"In the beauty of transformation is where memory truly lives.

"By weaving interconnections and braiding disparate stories together into garments, design becomes a way of operating, an interlaced, intertwined web that helps us exist within a complicated world."

Student: Miranda Kistler
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutor: Jacqueline Loekito

All These Open Windows But No Fresh Air by Nada Elghareb

"The project presents a portable, pocket-sized sensory hunting game. The game aims to ground the player in the physical world through tactile tasks.

"It functions either as a standalone screen-free companion or as a magnetic attachment for your smartphone."

Student: Nada Elghareb
Course: Studio Industrial Design

Noerah by Noerah

"The NOERAH FW26 debut collection plays with the idea of 'accessorise until you're dressed' as both method and attitude.

"It is an exploration of accessories not as additions, but as the starting point from which garments emerge.

"NOERAH's world revolves around wearable objects, attachments and bodily extensions that activate and involve the body.

"Influenced by electronic music, club culture, post-human feminism and avatar-based styling games, the collection proposes a universe of wearable fantasies, shifting identities, synthetic glamour and collective imagination."

Student: Noerah
Course: Studio Fashion
Tutors: Jacqueline Loekito, Prof. Priska Morger and Ruth Scheel

MOOVE – A new perspective on mobility for older adults by Lorenzo Rimini

"Aging is often treated as a problem to solve rather than a natural phase of life. Yet society remains largely designed around young, able-bodied users, creating dependency and reduced confidence among older adults.

"MOOVE responds to this gap by introducing an 'aging travel companion' for active travellers aged 75 plus. Positioned between luggage and a walker, it combines walking support, a perching seat and contemporary aesthetics.

"Each function supports a sense of autonomy: stability enables confidence, seating provides reliability and personalisation preserves dignity. Rather than assisting users as patients, MOOVE empowers them to travel independently, confidently and with style."

Student: Lorenzo Rimini
Course: Studio Industrial Design

item.content:encoded:
A sweeping white roof informed by the pages of a book crowns Chang'an Academy Xi'an Public Library, a cultural centre in Shanxi Province.

Overlooking the Ba River and Olympic Sports Centre in Xi'an's Chanba Ecological Area, the 70,000-square-metre complex contains spaces for reading, exhibitions and education.

It was designed by Chinese studios Hong Designworks and China Northwest Architectural Design and Research Institute.

The design team looked to balance the project's role as a large-scale public landmark with spaces that would feel welcoming and accessible to visitors, describing their approach as a process of "de-memorialisation."

"Our inspiration came from observing a shift in how public cultural architecture is being discussed today," Hong Designworks co-founder Ming Dang told Dezeen.

"The focus is no longer solely on formal expression, but increasingly on how spaces invite everyday use."

"The vitality of cultural architecture, we believe, lies not in scale alone, but in its capacity to sustain genuine, everyday connections between people and the city," Dang continued.

In order to help break down the scale of the building, it is divided into three sections by a central plaza and a long, narrow cut made through its centre, drawing both visitors and daylight into a large atrium.

According to Hong Designworks, this atrium was designed to encourage a wide range of activities, from quieter working areas and reading nooks to amphitheatre-style spaces for larger gatherings.

These are organised across a variety of levels and connected by curved staircases and walkways.

Read:

Sinuous form of Shenzhen Natural History Museum emulates "a piece of landscape"

"In many large-scale public buildings, atria are often conceived as monumental voids – spaces intended primarily for circulation rather than lingering," said Dang.

"The project breaks away from this 'large but empty' spatial logic, transforming the atrium into an engaging environment that encourages gathering, pause, and interaction."

Enhancing the feeling of openness in these spaces is the library's sweeping roof, which is lower at the building's centre and rises upwards in its corners above full-height glazed walls.

As well as evoking the pages of an open book, this form was chosen as a nod to the upturned eaves found in traditional Chinese architecture.

Wood-grain metal panels were used throughout the interiors to satisfy fire requirements while maintaining a feeling of warmth, alongside stone floors and ceilings clad in white triangular panels.

Other libraries in China recently featured in Dezeen include the Beijing City Library by Snøhetta, which features a roof designed to emulate the feeling of "sitting under a tree", and a library designed to resemble a shell made from bricks.

The photography is courtesy of Studio Ten.

item.content:encoded:
Paint brand Dulux has announced Soulful Sage – "a versatile green that provides a flexible foundation for schemes" – as its colour of the year for 2027.

Dulux selected the soft grey-green as its annual colour of the year as it is a calm shade that has clear connections to nature.

"Taking us straight back to nature, it's a calm, uplifting shade – just what's needed today," the brand said.

The selection is the result of research carried out throughout the year by the paint brand's parent company AkzoNobel. According to the brand, sage is a soothing and versatile colour, chosen as a response to the current feelings of global uncertainty.

"To deliver projects that add lasting value, architects, specifiers and designers must consider how colour can support the intended purpose of a space, its functionality and the experience of the people using it," said Dulux.

"AkzoNobel's annual ColourFutures research helps to inform this by translating emerging social and design trends into a practical colour direction that professionals can interpret and adapt for real projects."

Read:

Rhythm of Blues named Dulux Colour of the Year 2026

"For 2027, the research identified a move towards lighter, more considered environments that respond to the information overload and wider global uncertainty that people are experiencing," the brand continued.

"These insights shaped Soulful Sage, a versatile green that provides a flexible foundation for schemes requiring different levels of warmth, neutrality or visual energy, depending on the brief."

Last year Dulux selected a trio of blue colours named Rhythm of Blues, as its Colour of the Year.

Rival colour arbiter Pantone, meanwhile, picked an understated, greyish white hue called Cloud Dancer.

Dezeen Showroom: HIMACS has added five colourways to its terrazzo-inspired collection, which have received a prestigious Red Dot Design Award 2026 in the product category.

The HIMACS Terrazzo collection reimagines a timeless material technique through rich textures, a carefully balanced colour palette and distinctive, mineral-inspired patterns.

The five additional HIMACS Terrazzo colours include Terrazzo Ulivo, Terrazzo Nuvola, Terrazzo Sorrento, Terrazzo Marsala and Terrazzo Selva.

The latest colours have been recognised with the award, which celebrates the contemporary reinterpretation of traditional aesthetics, combining expressive design with responsible material innovation.

The hues incorporate SCS-certified pre-consumer recycled content, demonstrating how the demands of modern design can successfully coexist with enhanced sustainability in a high-performance solid surface.

The result is a versatile surface solution suited to hospitality, retail, workplace and residential environments. It also boasts the same aesthetics, durability and ease-of-maintenance that terrazzo is famous for.

"The integration of production offcuts, recovered and reintroduced into new formulations during the fabrication process, supports a more circular approach to manufacturing," said Martin Saxby, director of HIMACS UK.

"Among the awarded colours, Terrazzo Selva stands out with 25 per cent recycled content, one of the highest levels currently available within our extensive portfolio," Saxby added.

"Safety is a further consideration when specifying materials, and HIMACS is entirely free of silica, nanoparticles, formaldehyde and VOCs," he continued.

item.content:encoded:
Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind has been named architecture laureate for this year's Praemium Imperiale awards by the Japan Art Association.

Libeskind, who leads the New York-based Studio Libeskind and is one of the judges for this year's Dezeen Awards, was selected for the award for his work creating "emotionally resonant, innovative, and sustainable" architecture.

"Daniel Libeskind is an internationally renowned architect and urban designer, celebrated for his ability to evoke cultural memory through emotionally resonant and original architecture," the Japan Art Association said.

"Guided by a deep passion for music, philosophy, and literature, Libeskind creates architecture that is emotionally resonant, innovative, and sustainable."

Born in Łódź, Poland, in 1946, Libeskind is known for his deconstructionist style, which favours sharp angles and geometric structures.

Notable projects by the architect include the Jewish Museum Berlin in 2001 and Bundeswehr Museum of Military History in 2011.

More recently, the studio completed the Maggie's Centre at the Royal Free in London and the Atrium at Sumner in Brooklyn, New York.

Alongside his built works, the awarding body also praised Libeskind's wider contributions to architectural education and his influence on shaping cultural spaces.

"Libeskind is also a prominent voice in the field, frequently speaking at universities and professional conferences on the art and impact of architecture," the Japan Art Association said.

"His work and ideas have been featured in numerous exhibitions and publications, shaping contemporary architectural discourse and influencing the evolution of cities and cultural spaces."

Libeskind will receive an honorarium of 15 million yen (£70,000) as the winner of the architecture award, which is given out annually by the Japan Art Association under the patronage of Prince Hitachi, younger brother to the emperor emeritus of Japan.

Read:

Kengo Kuma awarded Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award by CDA

The Praemium Imperiale is an annual global arts prize that celebrates creatives in the fields of architecture, painting, sculpture, music, theatre and film.

Named alongside Libeskind as this year's winners are actor Cate Blanchett for theatre and film and artists Herbert Blomstedt for music, Andy Goldsworthy for sculpture and Jenny Holzer for painting. All were praised for their creative impact on society.

"This year's laureates share an immense passion for their respective craft as well as the land and people that inspire their art," Praemium Imperiale's International Advisor in the UK Lord Patten of Barnes said.

"Together their body of work celebrates the beauty and transformative power of art for the individual and the society."

Alongside the Praemium Imperiale Awards, the Japan Art Association selected children's art network La Source Garouste for the 2026 Grant for Young Artists.

Previous winners of the award's architecture category include Eduardo Souto de Moura, Shigeru Ban and Diébédo Francis Kéré.

The photography is by Roland Horn, courtesy of the Japan Art Association, unless otherwise stated.

item.content:encoded:
Students at Finland's Aalto University have collaborated with Dutch pram brand Bugaboo to create a pushchair using bio-based and biodegradable materials.

Amsterdam brand Bugaboo originally approached Aalto University during last year's Dutch Design Week, where the school presented an exhibition of experimental biomaterials.

To translate some of this biomaterial innovation into a functioning product, students from the Espoo institution's multidisciplinary chemarts course joined forces with the design team at Bugaboo.

The result is a version of the brand's stroller that's decked out in biodegradable materials but retains Bugaboo's classic black metal frame, including the wheels and seat belts.

"Sometimes, it's the unexpected or seemingly crazy ideas that open up new possibilities and start important conversations," Aalto University design professor Anna-Marie van der Lei told Dezeen.

"We need to imagine and experiment with what our future material world could look like, whether that means creating canopies from peels or foams from egg cartons."

Chemical engineering student Nikolai Kurochkin developed a composite material of sawdust and methyl cellulose that forms a sandy-hued back panel for the pushchair. Methyl cellulose is a compound derived from plant cellulose that can be used as a thickener and emulsifier.

The brown-coloured, plant-based leather seat cover was created by Alois Auer and Renata Khayrutdinova, who coated the material in tar to make it as water-repellent as possible.

"The students developed the tar coating that gives the seat a pleasant scent as well as durability," explained bio products professor Tiina Nypelö.

"With fully biodegradable materials, achieving water resistance is challenging," added van der Lei, who conceded that a fully waterproof biomaterial pram is still a work in progress.

The seat cover was inlaid with a mixture of materials to provide cushioning. Starch-based foam by Nooa Laisalmi was combined with recycled fibre-foam stuffing created by Elisabeth Baidoo from egg cartons that would have otherwise been thrown away.

Read:

Finnish company launches "world's most carbon-storing building material"

For the pram's woven canopy, Serranur Zileli developed a light brown material made from waste orange peel, which emits a subtle citrusy smell.

Julia Särkkä designed a delicate, biolace blanket in the same colour using hemp and lignin – one of the key polymers that give strength and durability to plant cell walls.

The pushchair's product labels are also cellulose-based, developed by Alessandra Fini, Bianca-Elena Galan and Cathrin Simbikangwa.

The pram was developed in Aalto University's Chemarts laboratory, with each student using specific processes and equipment depending on the biomaterial they were conceiving.

While the pushchair is currently only a concept model, the professors said that working with Bugaboo offered students the chance to work in a real-world context.

"Students had opportunities to meet with Bugaboo's design lead and engineer and discuss their experiments," said Van der Lei.

"Bugaboo gave us a lot of freedom, and the final stroller was developed by students who chose to continue working on the project themselves."

Known for championing biomaterials, researchers at Aalto University recently salvaged 300-year-old wood from the wreckage of a cargo ship in Oulu, which was transformed into yarn and knitted into a zero-waste dress.

A slew of other projects exploring the potential of cellulose have been showcased at the institution in previous years.

The photography is by Esa Kapila, courtesy of Aalto University.

item.content:encoded:
Chairs made of wood lacquer and a lighting installation informed by paper-twining were among the highlights of the In Situ exhibition during Design Miami Seoul.

Taking place from 31 August to 6 September, this year's Design Miami Seoul was held at Design Lab within the Zaha Hadid-designed Dongdaemun Design Plaza.

Its In Situ exhibition spotlighted Korean design from both emerging and established studios, spanning lighting, furniture, ceramics, and sculptural design.

Here Dezeen selects seven of the most interesting designs from In Situ:

Biiit collection by Mano Design Studio

This brass structure was designed to be a contemporary reinterpretation of traditional Korean candlesticks, with paper made from raw mulberry bark  stitched around the frame.

Seoul-based Mano Design Studio was founded by Bo Ah Kim in 2016, who works at the intersection of traditional Korean craft and contemporary design.

"The Biiit collection seeks to dissolve the hierarchy between maker and material in an era of uniform mass replication," said Kim.

"Through a relational resonance built on mutual engagement, it aims to restore design's inherent, tactile 'thingness'."

Narrative series, by Byungsub Kim

Seoul-based furniture designer Byungsub Kim designed a chair, shelving unit and bench for his Narrative series collection.

Kim combined stainless steel with Korean mother of pearl lacquerware – a traditional craft in which wood is lacquered and inlaid with mother of pearl – for the pieces.

"The Narrative series illuminates the tension that exists among the passage of time harboured within materials, the remnants of discarded functions, and their newly bestowed roles," said Kim.

After Inage series and White Nostalgia series, by Hyunhee Kim

Artist Hyunhee Kim developed a series of furniture informed by traditional Korean furniture and gyubang culture – the material and domestic culture associated with women's quarters in the traditional Korean home.

For the pieces, she deconstructed classical furniture forms and combined contemporary sculptural language with modern materials such as acrylic and aluminium, creating a dialogue between past and present.

Nodus, by Il Hoon Roh

Nodus is a lighting installation by Seoul-based architect Il Hoon Roh, which was informed by Korean's traditional paper-twining technique that first appeared in the 12th century.

Contemporary materials such as carbon fibre was combined with the heritage craft. Individual strands were twisted into knots which then accumulated to form a surface.

The work was created through the repetitive act of knotting, in reference to the name of the piece Nodus, which means knot in Latin.

"The series represent both an artistic investigation into the evolving relationship between these disciplines and a compelling synthesis of traditional craftsmanship and cutting-edge contemporary materials," said Roh.

Guseul by WKND Lab

Design studio WKND Lab's Guseul (sphere in Korean) is a lighting installation that featured a series of balls crafted by various traditional Korean techniques.

The black balls were made using Ottchil and mother of pearl, traditional wood lacquer inlaid with mother of pearl, while the red Chil-bo balls used a glass enamel technique and were made in collaboration with artisan Jeongkeun Park.

Founded by Eunji Jun and Halin Lee, WKND Lab aims to preserve traditional values by integrating them into contemporary work.

"Guseul embodies the journey from a single dot to a profound line, symbolising the connection of diverse elements into a cohesive whole," said WKND Lab.

Chimi Chair by Mokamjunamoo

Design studio Mokamjunamoo presented Chimi Chair at the exhibition. It was informed by chimi, a sculptural element found at the ends of the ridge lines in traditional Korean wooden architecture.

"Chimi Chair functions both as a utilitarian object and as an exploration of how the sculptural language of traditional architecture can be translated into a contemporary, everyday context," said Mokamjunamoo founder of Hwan Tae Kim.

Drawing in Space, by Cheon Woosun

Metal artist Cheon Woosun created vessel-like forms by welding metal wires with silver.

Drawing from the shape of Korean ceramic jars, the vessels were formed by connecting individual wires, which the Woosun described as "sketching in pencil".

Design Miami Seoul 2026 took place from 31 August to 6 September 2026 at Design Lab within Dongdaemun Design Plaza, Seoul, South Korea. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

item.content:encoded:
The construction of a 250-foot-high triumphal arch in Washington DC designed by Atlanta-based Harrison Design, is set to begin "over the next two-week period".

Plans to begin construction of the giant arch, alongside the Arlington Memorial Bridge on the south bank of the Potomac River, were announced last week by US interior secretary Doug Burgum.

"We are pleased to announce that after a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the great triumphal arch and military observation deck, at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery," he wrote on X (formerly Twitter).

"This will be one of the Great Pieces of American architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful capital in the World."

Officially called the Triumphal Arch of Washington DC, the structure is one of numerous additions being made to the city by US president Donald Trump.

Nicknamed the "Arc de Trump" – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris – the arch will be nearly 100 feet (30 metres) taller than its Parisian counterpart.

The arch, which was approved by the US Commission of Fine Arts in May, was designed by Atlanta-based studio Harrison Design. It will be neoclassical in style and topped by three gilded angels.

Within the structure will be three floors of accessible space to allow the structure to be a visitor attraction.

Read:

"Arc de Trump" design approved for Washington DC

On the ground floor will be a space for ticketing and security, with spiral staircases and lifts giving access to the upper floors.

Four galleries for exhibitions, along with restrooms, will be located within the main attic space, with the open-air observation deck above.

The arch is one of several major construction projects led by Trump that are currently underway in the US capital city.

The most significant of which, the addition of a ballroom to the White House, is moving forward after the US Supreme Court ruled that construction can continue.

The imagery is by Harrison Design via CFA.

Dezeen Showroom: Italian manufacturer Iris Ceramica Group has recreated the warm elegance of an unmistakable pink Italian marble in its Breccia Rosa 4D slab tile.

Produced by its subsidiary Sapienstone, the Breccia Rosa 4D porcelain stoneware tile emulates the look of its namesake marble, which is also known as Breccia Pernice or Breccia Oniciata and is quarried around Verona.

Like the finest slabs of this type, it has an even antique pink colour with sprawling ivory veins and traces of terracotta, powder pink and grey adding depth.

Iris Ceramica Group manufactures the large-format tile using its 4D technology so that the colour and pattern runs throughout the body of the slab, allowing for seamless edges.

The company recommends the product for applications including worktops, cladding and surfaces, where its durability and resistance supports daily use and its velvety Cashmere finish invites touch.

"Pink is one of the most significant colours in contemporary design," said Iris Ceramica Group. "It has entered residential and high-end contract architecture palettes as a sign of a return to warm materials and intimate spaces."

"Breccia Rosa captures this moment, bringing a warm colour into a complex form capable of interacting with and enhancing other materials within a space."
