item.content:encoded:
A thousand tonnes of volcanic rock replace concrete and steel in Petra Heights, a housing development in north London by architecture studio Groupwork and engineer Webb Yates.

The apartment building at 317 Finchley Road consists of three blocks ranging from six to 10 storeys, all held up by an exoskeleton of unreinforced stone.

This ladder frame single-handedly carries the high-rise's weight and wind loads, with no concrete stability core or concrete columns, no steel reinforcement bars and no need for cladding since the stone acts as both structure and facade.

"All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone," said Webb Yates co-founder Steve Webb, who describes the solution as a "world-first". "If the stone wasn't here, it would be a pile of rubble," he added.

Made of Sicilian basalt and Norwegian larvikite, the frame's post-and-lintel construction follows the same logic as Groupwork and Webb Yates's controversial Stirling Prize-shortlisted 15 Clerkenwell Close.

While the previous building was shorter, at six-storeys, it still relied on a concrete core to steady it against the wind. Petra Heights eliminates this emissions-intensive building element entirely.

"It's really escalating an idea," Webb told Dezeen. "So Clerkwell is a load-bearing exoskeleton, Finchley Road is load bearing exoskeleton stability structure, and then if we build another one, it can be taller, higher, stronger."

The building represents the latest step in the studios' ongoing, 15-year mission to establish stone as a viable, low-carbon alternative for steel and concrete, which together account for 16 per cent of humanity's emissions.

Load-bearing stone is second only to carbon-sequestering timber in its sustainability, they argue, and can cut the embodied carbon footprint of a building's superstructure by up to 95 per cent if quarried in the same country.

"This is what any architect and engineer should be doing," Groupwork founder Amin Taha told Dezeen. "Start off with timber. Where can the timber not be used? Then the next material should be stone because it's so low in embodied carbon."

Crucially, stone can also go where mass timber can't, which according to UK fire regulations is any building above 18 metres.

The exoskeleton that holds up Petra Height, on the other hand, could be scaled up to build a 30-storey skyscraper, which could cut emissions by 80 per cent compared to a steel frame at no additional cost, research from Groupwork and Webb Yates suggests.

"Finchley Road is interesting in its own right, but it's more interesting because it's a kind of stepping stone to some bigger changes and a kind of demonstration project of what can be done," Webb explained.

Set on a tricky site between a train station and the six-lane artery of Finchley Road, Petra Heights still relies on concrete basement foundations and floor slabs, as well as imported stone.

But its carbon footprint from materials and construction remains around 32 per cent less than that of a comparable reinforced-concrete structure, the studios said.

Using a stone-and-timber flooring system – as the studios had originally planned – could've pushed the savings up to 75 per cent.

To limit transport emissions, the original aim was to build Petra Heights from local rock. But at the time of the project's inception, just three years after Clerkenwell Close, the duo struggled to find a UK quarry excavating large enough pieces of strong enough stone to create the building's 572 columns and beams, the largest of which is five metres long.

Instead, the team pivoted to Sicilian basalt, manually split and cut into shape by Italian stonemason Ateliers Romeo using a computerised diamond-wire saw and a spreadsheet breaking down the exact dimensions of every block.

As construction dragged on over the pandemic, that quarry, too, struggled to create bigger pieces, and the team switched to larvikite from Norway's Lundhs quarry – the company's first structural stone project for almost 100 years since supplying the columns for Oslo's public library in 1933.

Read:

Design Museum pushes for stone construction in the UK with Stone Demonstrator

"Probably today, if this came to the drawing board, we wouldn't make it in very large pieces of stone like that," Webb said. "We'd tension up smaller pieces because you don't have to find a special quarry with especially strong, large pieces of stone."

"You could actually use UK stone, piece it together in this country, so you don't have to transport it for long distances, and it's cheaper because you're not finding that special quarry," he continued.

Basalt was used for the building's lower storeys, while the larvikite can be seen on the upper storeys, the tallest of which reaches up to 30 metres above ground.

To unify these different volcanic rocks, Groupwork used a chemical wash to oxidise the stone and bring out its iron content. This is what gives the building its distinctive rusty colour, blending in with the area's historic red-brick homes.

Similar techniques have been used by stonemasons for generations in restoration projects to match freshly cut stone to the existing structure, according to Taha.

"It used to be called soot-washing, so you would get soot from a chimney and mix it and brush it across stone to make it look older," he said.

In total, the exoskeleton consists of more than 1,000 tonnes of stone, joined together using steel dowels and brackets plus some epoxy mortar.

To reduce the building's mass and maximise its awkwardly shaped site, the structure is split into three blocks that, between them, house 22 apartments plus a glass-fronted shop set behind a colonnade on the ground floor.

Groupwork also decided to chamfer back the top few storeys of all three blocks so they can't be seen from the surrounding conservation areas.

Petra Heights' upper storeys – and the roof gardens set atop the two shorter blocks – can be accessed via a lightweight open-air staircase and an elevator at the heart of the plan.

Made from prefabricated stone modules, dropped in one on top of the other, the lift shaft was erected in just a day and a half, in what Webb believes might be another world's first. An adjoining riser core, housing utilities and services, was constructed of 2,400 stone bricks.

"This has shown that an ordinary general contractor can very easily develop methodologies and procedures to build a stone structure without needing somebody who's done 50 years of apprenticeship carving the stone of Notre Dame or whatever," he said.

Taha and Webb argue that Petra Heights's load-bearing stone exoskelleton offers a "far more interesting, more sustainable, more ethical kind of architecture" than the brick-clad buildings that have come to dominate UK architecture in recent years, accounting for five of the six projects on this year's Stirling Prize shortlist.

They hope it can serve as a model for how the 1.5 million new homes the government has promised to deliver by 2029 could be built in a more sustainable way.

"Building a million homes in our vernacular housing typology, which is fake brick stuck on concrete frame, is an environmental catastrophe," Webb said.

"The impact of removing the concrete core from high rises, has a big carbon benefit," he continued. "And I think the applicability of that in the UK for all medium rise housing – get rid of all the brickwork, get rid of all the concrete cores from concrete medium rise housing – will put a big dent in the carbon footprint of the million homes."

In upcoming projects, including a recently greenlit development in Hackney, Groupwork and Webb Yates are already planning to bring down their use of steel and concrete even further.

The project, which Taha self-financed by selling his home and office in Clerkenwell Close, aims to go carbon negative by cutting out concrete almost entirely with the help of stone foundations and the stone-and-timber flooring system they had intended for Petra Heights.

item.content:encoded:
Britain's design industry has grown by 40 per cent and is now responsible for £1 in every £20 generated across the country, according to a landmark report from the Design Council.

Published today, the report paints a positive picture of a thriving design industry, which contributed £136.7 billion in gross value added (GVA) to the UK economy in 2023 – a 40 per cent rise from 2019.

As a result, the design industry has overtaken the £114 billion retail sector as the single biggest contributor to the national economy, the report argues.

It is now almost twice the size of the £70 billion accommodation and food service industry, and responsible for around £1 in every £20 generated nationwide.

The sector has also outpaced the UK economy as a whole, which grew by only 24 per cent over the same period.

"80 per cent of designers work in other parts of the economy"

Ahead of the report's publication, the Design Council's chief design officer Cat Drew spoke to Dezeen about the findings.

"Design is an essential business capability across industries with designers operating across the whole of the economy, from urban planning to computer games," she said.

"We classify some designers as working in design industries, in businesses such as architecture firms or fashion houses, but 80 per cent of designers work in other parts of the economy," Drew added.

"For example, healthcare providers such as the NHS now have digital teams, and financial service providers rely on in-house designers to create new products and services."

The report also found that the design economy has seen a 15 per cent increase in employment since 2020 – adding around 297,000 jobs – and currently supports 2.27 million jobs.

During this period, total UK employment grew by less than 2.5 per cent, highlighting the comparative expansion of the design sector.

The Design Council also found that design-led growth is being felt beyond London and the southeast of the UK, regions historically afforded the most creative opportunities.

Since 2019, the council reported an 88 per cent increase in design's economic contribution in Wales, a 67 per cent increase in the northeast and a 32 per cent increase in Scotland.

AI could present a threat to future growth

While these results point to a thriving industry, Drew acknowledged that it "is possible that we have captured a peak in the trend", considering the potential impacts of artificial intelligence (AI).

"It's likely too early to see the effect of AI on the design workforce in the medium-term data trend, from 2020 to 2025, and when looking at the design economy as a whole," she said.

A survey from the World Economic Forum previously found that graphic design is considered one of the jobs most at risk from AI, while the demand for UX and UI designers is expected to grow.

Early indications in the Design Council report seem to reflect this trend.

"When we look more granularly, growth in graphic design slowed between 2023 and 2025," she continued. "Digital design by comparison has seen a boom, now accounting for 59 per cent of the whole design economy and growing by 26 per cent to over 1 million people employed."

"If you're 16 today, studying design isn't only training to become a graphic designer in a design studio," added Drew.

"It's developing the ability to understand people, frame problems, generate solutions and turn ideas into things that work and those capabilities require human sensibilities that AI cannot replace."

Design needs a "more diverse talent pipeline"

Drew also acknowledged AI as a possible threat to the next generation of designers, with automation chipping away at entry-level opportunities that traditionally help young people get a foot in the door.

Risks to the future skills pipeline also emerge earlier on in education, with 68 per cent fewer students taking the Design and Technology (D&T) GCSE course between 2014 and 2024, while the number of D&T teachers was halved.

Drew emphasised the sustained lack of sufficient progress towards workforce diversity as another key pillar of the report.

Read:

Big-name studios encouraging architects to use AI

"Our new findings show that only two per cent of designers were female in 2025 and only two per cent of designers were Black, compared to five per cent in the UK workforce," she said.

"We need to attract a more diverse talent pipeline if the products, services, buildings and public spaces they produce are to be truly inclusive and accessible."

Last year, the Design Council hosted the World Design Congress, which took place in London.

The biennial event included a keynote speech by architect Norman Foster on the importance of walkable cities, and another talk with musician Brian Eno, who emphasised the importance of communities in the design world.

Dezeen Showroom: Italian brand Ceramiche Keope has recreated the subtle allure of limestone in its Grace collection of porcelain stoneware tiles.

The Grace collection was created with reference to limestone from the region of Saint Antoine d'Auberoche in France, a popular source of stone for European buildings throughout the 19th century.

Ceramiche Keope mimics its understated elegance with a look that appears near uniform from a distance but reveals the mesmerising detail of grains of sand and small fossils when viewed up close.

The colour palette is also drawn from the stone of this region, with options ranging from pure White to earthy Clay and grey Iron — each containing limestone's quiet interplay of warm and cool tones.

The Grace collection is suitable for both indoors and outdoors, in residential, commercial and public settings, and comes in a range of natural-look and anti-slip finishes.

There are also a number of decorative designs in the collection, such as the engraving-inspired Weave, which features light intersecting lines in an art deco-style pattern.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture collective Badweather has transformed a 17-metre canal boat into Soak, an off-grid bathhouse that moves to a new location along London's waterways every two weeks.

Soak combines a wood-fired sauna, two cold plunge pools, showers, changing facilities and a small bar for up to 12 people.

It operates without mains water, electricity or sewage connections, instead drawing water directly from the canal and passing it through a six-stage filtration and UV treatment system before it is used for bathing.

Electricity is generated by solar panels and stored in an onboard battery system, while a wood-fired stove provides heat for the sauna.

The project was developed by Badweather co-founder Leo Sixsmith and chef and former restaurateur Riccardo Codacci-Pisanelli, who wanted to create a communal bathing space that could move through the city rather than occupy a permanent site.

"The changing location of the boat means that the view through these windows is never the same," Sixsmith told Dezeen.

Soak began with a near-derelict 20-year-old canal boat, with rotten floors, water damage and a steel hull that required extensive restoration. Around 40 people worked on its conversion, with the existing hull dictating much of the interior layout.

The exterior was painted cream with black and red detailing, while circular portholes puncture the sides of the boat.

Read:

Future Simple Studio creates "contemporary vocabulary" for Montreal bathhouse

Inside, the original 11-inch openings have been enlarged to 18 and 32 inches, with fiery-red frames that make the windows stand out against the hull.

At the bow, a large picture window replaces an original steel door, opening the narrow interior towards the water.

The interior follows the boat's long, narrow form. Visitors enter through a dark changing and reception area lined with stained marine plywood. They then pass into a brighter plunge and shower room, featuring pale green tiles, stainless-steel pools and a central skylight that brings daylight into the boat.

"The wet room is intentionally kept completely free of timber," Sixsmith said. "Its harder, clinical finish allows for easier maintenance, while heightening the sensory contrast with the warmth of the sauna."

At the bow, the sauna is lined with thermally treated Aspen and Alder wood and is centred around a wood-burning stove.

Two benches were suspended from aluminium beams rather than supported by legs, allowing them to overlap within the tapered hull.

The boat's cramped dimensions were a major constraint, but Badweather aimed to use them to shape the interior. "Every centimetre had to work exceptionally hard," Sixsmith said.

Founded in London in 2019 by Oli Brenner, Sophie Mei Birkin and Sixsmith, Badweather is an experimental architecture, scenography and design collective working across installations, objects, lighting and buildings.

Its previous work includes temporary structures for nightclubs and festivals, including the ongoing Pipeline project, a floating communal hearth made from reused corrugated polycarbonate.

Other bathhouses featured on Dezeen include a communal sauna and hydrotherapy bathhouse in Montreal and the turquoise-tiled Komaeyu public bathhouse in the suburbs of Tokyo.

The photography is by Kaye Song.
